meta.blurb: Isla Marlowe's phone rings in a kitchen drawer and her supper goes cold. Her workshop clock has stopped at twenty to ten, and the town whispers about her husband. Her sister Hannah remembers a childhood game, and starts looking for a clue.
meta.bible: Hannah Reed: Isla's younger sister, a schoolteacher, clever and loyal, our point of view. Isla Marlowe: a clock restorer who works for Gideon Pryce; maiden name Reed. Owen Marlowe: Isla's husband, a quiet accountant at Dunn and Hale. Gideon Pryce: owner of Pryce Antiques, silver hair, smooth voice; sells stolen clocks with forged papers. Mabel Cray: Pryce's frightened young assistant. Rufus Dray: Pryce's big, silent driver, who drives the green van and later the Gannet. Inspector Dana Okoye: the calm police detective. Constable Priya Nair: her young helper. Mr Doyle: the old neighbour with a terrier who saw the green van. Reverend Joan Bright: the vicar of Saint Brannock's church. Miss Agnes Penhale: Isla's old teacher, who lives on Gull Island near the lighthouse in a cottage with a blue door. Sam Tully: the old ferryman, whose ferry is the Kittiwake. Alma Finch: runs Finch's Cafe on the harbour and is kind to Owen. Larry Voss: reporter of the Saltmere Gazette. Mr Dunn: Owen's employer at Dunn and Hale. Leonard Quill: a retired solicitor who owns Thomas Reed's old workshop. Thomas Reed: the sisters' late father, a clockmaker, who died two years ago. Saltmere: the small seaside town. Marsh Street: where Isla and Owen live. Cobble Row: where Isla's own small workshop stands, five minutes from home. Gull Island: reached by the last ferry, which leaves at twenty to ten in festival week. Anchor Lane: where Thomas Reed's old workshop stands. Thornby: the village beyond which Pryce rents a barn. Thornby Farm: where Isla once hid in the hay as a child. Lantern Festival: the town's night of paper lanterns, postponed for two weeks. Saint Brannock's: the church whose turret clock was stolen last April. Gannet: the hired fishing boat Pryce uses to reach the island. Tick and Hide: the sisters' childhood game; the hider stops a clock and the time names a place on a timetable. Facts: the workshop clock was stopped at twenty to ten, the ferry time; the green van has a pale stripe; the red scarf was knitted by Hannah and left on the sea wall by Isla; Isla's grey raincoat with a hood is missing from its hook; Owen was saving cash in envelopes to buy back the old workshop; the lighthouse lamp is lit only on festival nights and has ninety-nine steps; Isla took the brass maker's plate from the stolen church clock and copied Pryce's account book; the sisters quarrelled at Christmas a year ago over Isla working for Pryce, and did not speak for a year. Voice and tone: tense, warm and clear, a fair-play mystery; no violence or gore; Isla is alive and Pryce is arrested.

beats.scene: A silver-haired man in an armchair speaks with pride about clocks
beats.summary: Isla keeps Pryce talking and he boasts of the church clock's craftsmanship.

beats.scene: A woman slips out of a cottage back door into the dusk
beats.summary: Hannah slips out of the back door with the key.

beats.scene: A woman runs across dark moorland toward a tall pale lighthouse
beats.summary: She runs through the dark heather to the lighthouse.

beats.scene: A spiral staircase of stone steps winds up inside a dark lighthouse
beats.summary: She climbs the ninety-nine steps to the lantern room.

beats.scene: A great lamp stands in a glass room beside a covered switch
beats.summary: She finds the old lamp and the switch behind glass, as Miss Penhale once showed her.

beats.scene: A powerful beam of light sweeps across a dark sea from a lighthouse
beats.summary: She throws the switch and the great beam sweeps over the sea.

beats.scene: A police inspector on a quay watches a beam of light
beats.summary: On the mainland Okoye sees the beam, knows the lamp burns only on festival nights and calls the launch.

beats.scene: A silver-haired man stares as a beam of light crosses a window
beats.summary: In the cottage Pryce sees the beam cross the window and understands.

beats.scene: A man grabs a biscuit tin from a sideboard in a panic
beats.summary: He snatches the tin and runs with Rufus for the boat.

beats.scene: An old woman closes a garden gate in front of a big man
beats.summary: Owen runs after them and Miss Penhale shuts the garden gate.

beats.scene: A woman runs down steep steps inside a lighthouse tower in the dark
beats.summary: Hannah hurries down the ninety-nine steps toward the shouting.

beats.scene: A man blocks a narrow stone jetty with his arms spread wide
beats.summary: Pryce reaches the jetty but Owen gets there first and blocks the narrow way.

beats.scene: Two men face each other on a narrow wet jetty at night
beats.summary: Pryce orders Owen aside and Owen says no.

beats.scene: A big man sits down in a small boat as a blue light flashes
beats.summary: Rufus sees the blue light of the police launch and sits down in the Gannet, giving up.

beats.scene: A silver-haired man slips on wet boards and a tin falls
beats.summary: Pryce lunges, slips on the wet boards and drops the tin, and Owen puts his foot on it.

beats.scene: A police boat with a searchlight comes alongside a dark jetty
beats.summary: The police launch arrives and a searchlight finds them.

beats.scene: A police inspector steps ashore and speaks to a kneeling man
beats.summary: Okoye arrests Gideon Pryce and Owen hands her the plate.

beats.scene: A police inspector writes statements at a cottage table at night
beats.summary: That night at the cottage Okoye takes statements and Isla hands over the account book.

beats.scene: A calm inspector speaks sternly to a seated woman across a table
beats.summary: Okoye tells Isla she wasted police time but will not charge her, and admits she was right.

beats.scene: A pale young woman waits on the steps of a police station at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Mabel Cray is waiting at the police station.

beats.scene: A frightened young woman confesses to a police inspector in an office
beats.summary: Mabel confesses she helped change plates and told Pryce about the ferryman, and she will give evidence.

beats.scene: A police inspector holds a paper beside a magistrate's desk
beats.summary: With the plate and Mabel's statement Okoye gets her warrant for the Thornby barn.

beats.scene: Police open a barn door on a huge turret clock under blankets
beats.summary: Police open the barn and under blankets stands the great turret clock of Saint Brannock's.

beats.summary: The Reverend Joan Bright weeps to see the clock, and the plate fits it.

beats.scene: A newspaper front page headline lies on a table beside a pen

beats.scene: Neighbours bring pies and flowers to a garden gate
beats.summary: Neighbours bring pies to Marsh Street and Owen forgives them, though Hannah forgives more slowly.

beats.scene: A woman winds a tall clock in a hallway lined with clocks
beats.summary: At home the clocks tick again and Isla winds each one, then restarts the tall clock.

beats.scene: A man puts a brass key into a woman's hand in a workshop doorway
beats.summary: Owen gives Isla the key to the old workshop on Anchor Lane and she is stunned.

beats.scene: A woman runs her hand along an old workbench in a dusty shop
beats.summary: Together they walk into the workshop and Isla finds her initials carved in the doorframe.

beats.summary: At dawn the sisters sit on the sea wall with the red scarf and promise to keep no more secrets.

beats.summary: Volunteers, the vicar and Isla lift the turret clock back into the tower of Saint Brannock's.

beats.scene: A clockmaker steadies a long pendulum in a stone tower
beats.summary: Isla sets the pendulum swinging and the clock begins to tick for the first time since April.

beats.scene: Crowds on a harbour quay hold glowing paper lanterns at dusk
beats.summary: On the evening of the postponed festival, lanterns light the harbour.

beats.scene: A tall lighthouse sends a beam across dark water full of lantern light
beats.summary: Miss Penhale switches on the lighthouse lamp and the beam crosses the water.

beats.scene: Two sisters and a husband stand with upturned faces under a church tower clock
beats.summary: At ten o'clock Saint Brannock's clock strikes ten for the first time in months.

A1A2: On the train, Hannah read her sister's letter again.
The train stopped at Saltmere as the lamps came on.
Owen met her at the gate and took her heavy bag.
They walked past Pryce Antiques, where Isla worked every day.
Their house on Marsh Street was full of ticking clocks.
Supper waited on the table, but Isla did not come.
Owen called her phone, and it rang inside a drawer.
They hurried down Cobble Row to Isla's small workshop.
The tall clock in the corner had stopped at twenty to ten.
Owen telephoned the police, and Hannah could not sleep.
In the morning Hannah found Isla's passport still in the drawer.
Inspector Okoye arrived and went first to the workshop.
Okoye asked Owen about the last time he saw Isla.
Okoye asked Hannah if her sister's marriage was happy.
Hannah told the inspector about the quarrel with Isla.
Volunteers met at the harbour, and Alma Finch made hot tea.
A man found a red scarf on the sea wall.
Men from the sea rescue team searched the rocks and found nothing.
The festival was put off for two weeks, and the lanterns came down.
Alone that night, Hannah looked at the silent clock.
The local paper put Isla's face on its front page.
In the bakery, people stopped talking when Hannah walked in.
At Pryce Antiques, Gideon Pryce said Isla left at five.
Pryce said Isla was brilliant and offered money for posters.
Mabel whispered that Isla was upset about numbers in a book.
Hannah searched the workshop and found a hidden notebook.
The pages were full of long numbers and short dates.
Alma said Isla had asked about the stolen church clock.
Hannah lay awake and thought about numbers and a church clock.
Hannah wondered what her sister's husband was hiding.
Okoye said the bank showed cash taken out every month.
Owen said only that he would never hurt Isla.
Hannah argued with Owen, and he begged for more time.
Owen's boss told him to stay away from the office.
Reporters gathered outside the house, and Larry Voss knocked.
Larry said someone had sent him a tip about the cash.
Someone painted words on the gate, and Owen scrubbed them off.
Owen said Isla had been nervous for weeks, as if afraid.
Hannah called her school and arranged to stay in Saltmere.
Okoye asked about Isla's friends and moods, and Hannah knew little.
Old Mr Doyle told her about a green van with a stripe.
A big man waited in the van, and it left before dark.
Okoye had already noted the van, but it had no number.
Hannah walked to Anchor Lane and stood before her father's shop.
Their father taught two girls to love clocks and timetables.
They played Tick and Hide, where the clock showed the hiding place.
Once Isla hid in the hay, and the bus time told Hannah.
Hannah thought the stopped clock was a message for her.
She checked the buses and trains for twenty to ten.
Hannah decided to look inside the clock itself.
That night Hannah went quietly to the workshop with a torch.
She saw fresh scratches around the screws on the clock.
Behind the weights she found a small brass key.
The key had a tiny pendulum on it and fit no door.
She tried every drawer and cupboard, but none of them opened.
Their father used to hide things behind false walls.
She tapped the panels behind the shelves and heard a hollow sound.
The panel slid aside and showed a narrow cabinet with a lock.
The key fit, and inside were photographs of clocks.
Each photograph had two numbers, and one was crossed out.
Hannah checked, and the crossed-out numbers were in the notebook.
A newspaper cutting told of a church clock that was stolen.
The cutting named the maker and gave the clock's number.
Hannah understood that Isla was tracing stolen clocks.
At dawn she told Owen, and he wanted to go to Pryce.
Hannah stopped him, because they had no proof yet.
Okoye said it was interesting, but not yet proof.
Okoye was cross with Hannah for hiding the notebook.
At Saint Brannock's the vicar showed her the empty clock tower.
The vicar said Pryce had offered to buy the clock.
Hannah walked down the back lane behind Pryce Antiques.
In the yard stood a green van with a pale stripe.
The big man stared at her and slammed the van door.
Mabel hurried out and begged her not to come back.
Pryce smiled from the door and asked her in for tea.
In his office Pryce spoke about Owen's bank money.
Pryce hinted that clever people should not ask about old clocks.
Hannah left shaken, but sure that Pryce was afraid.
Outside she wrote down part of the van's number.
Okoye said Pryce's driver had visited Isla's workshop at dusk.
Hannah woke at night and saw a light on Cobble Row.
Hannah and Owen ran to the workshop and found the door broken.
The hidden cabinet was open and empty, and the photographs were gone.
In the alley there was a tyre mark and a smell of oil.
Okoye and Nair came and found a green thread on the door.
Hannah admitted she kept the notebook and brought it out.
Okoye asked who knew about the cabinet, and Hannah feared the answer.
Hannah blamed herself, and Owen comforted her kindly.
At dawn Larry Voss came, and Hannah gave him one line.
Okoye warned Hannah she was in danger and posted a guard.
At three in the morning Owen could not keep his secret.
He was saving cash to buy back her father's workshop.
He showed her a receipt book signed by Mr Quill.
Hannah said she was sorry for doubting him.
He had hidden it because it was a surprise for Isla.
Okoye visited Mr Quill, and every payment was confirmed.
Okoye said Owen was no longer her main worry.
Mr Dunn called Owen back to work, but Owen refused.
Owen said he meant to give Isla the key on festival night.
Owen whispered that they would find her if she wanted to be found.
Okoye said Pryce rented a barn near Thornby village.
Hannah and Owen drove to Thornby to look at the barn.
The barn had a shiny new lock and covered windows.
Through a crack Hannah saw a big iron wheel under blankets.
An engine roared, and they hid behind a hedge.
Rufus checked the lock and said the plate must be found.
Okoye said a glimpse and some words were not enough.
Okoye warned that Pryce would look for Isla too.
Hannah feared that Pryce would find Isla first.
On the last page Hannah found clock hands and three words.
At dawn Hannah stood by the sea wall where the scarf was found.
Beside the wall a small ferry waited at the harbour steps.
The notice board said the last boat left at twenty to ten.
Hannah understood the game: the time meant Gull Island.
She ran home and saw the empty hook in the hall.
Owen said Miss Penhale lived by the island lighthouse.
They found Sam Tully fixing ropes in the ferry shed.
Tully remembered a woman in a grey hood on the last boat.
Tully said nobody from the police had asked him.
Across the quay Mabel Cray watched them from a window.
Owen telephoned Okoye and left a message about the island.
Hannah packed the scarf, the key and the notebook.
They boarded the Kittiwake with a few other passengers.
Hannah remembered Isla as a girl while the island grew.
Owen was afraid that Isla might not want to see him.
They landed on the old stone steps in wind and gull cries.
A path led through heather, past sheep and low stone walls.
Hannah remembered school trips and the ninety-nine steps.
The lighthouse came in sight beside a cottage with smoke.
By the blue door hung a grey coat with a hood.
Miss Penhale opened the door and said she wondered how long they took.
Miss Penhale was tall and brisk, and told them to mind the clocks.
In the front room, Miss Penhale said someone had counted the days.
Isla stood in the doorway, alive, with her hair cut short.
Owen crossed the room and held her, while Hannah laughed and wept.
Isla said, you found my clock, and Hannah said, you stopped it.
Hannah was angry with Isla for the fear she caused, and Isla said sorry.
Owen told Isla the town had suspected him, and she was horrified.
Miss Penhale put the kettle on and said tea came before explanations.
Isla took a breath and said she would start with Gideon Pryce.
Isla said she first noticed strange numbers on clocks at the shop.
She checked old directories in the library and the numbers did not match.
She understood that real plates were swapped for new ones.
In the barn she found the church clock with its old plate on.
She took the plate home and copied Pryce's account book.
On Friday Pryce came to the workshop, found out and threatened her.
Isla pretended to agree and promised the plate on Monday.
She stopped the clock at twenty to ten and took the last boat.
She told no one, because Pryce was watching, and she had invited Hannah.
Isla showed the brass plate and the account book copy from her bag.
In Saltmere Mabel told Pryce about Hannah and Sam Tully.
Pryce paid Rufus and they sailed in a hired boat.
Owen begged Isla to come home, but she wanted to wait for Okoye.
Miss Penhale told them the lamp burned only on festival nights.
From the top of the hill Owen reached Okoye, who promised the police boat.
On the cliff the sisters made peace over their quarrel.
Isla said she took the job for money, and Hannah said sorry.
Owen cooked supper as the light faded, and an engine sounded.
Miss Penhale saw a small boat at the steps with two men aboard.
There was a knock at the blue door, and Pryce said good evening.
Pryce smiled and politely asked Isla for the plate.
Isla said she would get it, and asked him to sit and talk.
Hannah whispered to Miss Penhale, who pointed to the lighthouse key.
Isla kept Pryce talking, and he boasted about the church clock.
Hannah slipped out of the back door with the key.
She ran through the dark heather to the lighthouse.
She climbed the ninety-nine steps up to the lantern room.
She found the old lamp and the switch behind glass.
She threw the switch, and a great beam crossed the sea.
On the mainland Okoye saw the beam and called the launch.
In the cottage Pryce saw the beam cross the window.
Pryce snatched the tin and ran with Rufus for the boat.
Owen ran after them, and Miss Penhale shut the garden gate.
Hannah ran down the ninety-nine steps toward the shouting.
Owen reached the landing first and blocked the narrow way.
Pryce told Owen to move, and Owen said no.
Rufus saw the blue light of the launch and sat down.
Pryce lunged, slipped on the wet boards and dropped the tin.
The police boat arrived, and a bright light found them all.
Okoye arrested Gideon Pryce, and Owen handed her the plate.
That night Okoye took statements, and Isla gave her the account book.
Okoye said Isla had wasted police time, but would not be charged.
At dawn Mabel Cray was waiting on the steps of the police station.
Mabel confessed that she had changed plates and told Pryce everything.
With the plate and Mabel's words, Okoye got her warrant.
The police opened the barn, and the great church clock stood inside.
In the barn were crates of other clocks and a buyer's invoice.
The vicar wept to see the clock, and the plate fitted.
The Gazette cleared Owen, and Larry Voss wrote an apology.
Neighbours brought pies, and Owen was kind to them all.
At home Isla wound each clock and restarted the tall clock.
Owen gave Isla the key to her father's old workshop.
They went into the workshop, and Isla found her carved initials.
Hannah told them she had applied for a job at the Saltmere school.
At dawn the sisters sat on the wall and promised no more secrets.
Volunteers and the vicar lifted the old clock back into the tower.
Isla set the pendulum swinging, and the clock began to tick.
On festival night, lanterns lit up the whole harbour.
Miss Penhale switched on the lamp, and the beam crossed the water.
At ten o'clock Saint Brannock's clock struck ten once more.
B1B2: Hannah unfolds Isla's letter for the third time as the evening train rattles toward the coast. It is cheerful and warm, yet every sentence seems to have been chosen very carefully.
The train slows beside a harbour where men on ladders are hanging paper lanterns. Out on Gull Island the lighthouse stands dark, because its lamp will not be lit until the festival tomorrow night.

Owen is waiting by the station gate in his tidy coat, and he looks more tired than Hannah has ever seen him. He takes her bag without a word and tells her that Isla is still working and will be home soon.

They walk through streets hung with unlit lanterns and pass the window of Pryce Antiques, where Isla works. Hannah asks how the job is going, and Owen answers only that Isla has been working very late.
The house on Marsh Street is full of clocks, and every one of them ticks at a slightly different speed. Upstairs, the spare room has been made ready with clean sheets and a jug of yellow flowers.
On the kitchen table a fish pie waits under a cloth, with three plates laid beside it. They wait for an hour, and Owen keeps looking at the door as the pie goes cold.
At last Owen rings his wife's number, and a low buzzing starts somewhere in the kitchen. Hannah pulls open the drawer by the sink and finds Isla's phone lying among the spoons, still ringing.
Owen takes a torch from the hall and they hurry down Cobble Row, five minutes from the house. The workshop door stands ajar, and a yellow lamp is still burning inside.

Inside, the workbench is tidy, with a half-mended carriage clock lying open under the lamp. In the corner the tall clock stands perfectly still, its hands stopped at twenty to ten, and Isla is nowhere.

At midnight Owen telephones the police, and a tired voice says that somebody will call in the morning. Hannah lies awake in the spare room, listening to thirty clocks ticking and thinking of the one that was silent.
In the morning Hannah searches the whole house as quietly as she can. Isla's passport, purse and blue coat are all still here, and only one hook in the hall stands empty.
Inspector Dana Okoye arrives at nine with a young constable named Priya Nair. She is calm and unhurried, and she asks to see the workshop before she sits down.
At the kitchen table Okoye asks Owen to describe the last time he saw his wife. He says they had breakfast on Friday, that Isla was quiet, and that she kissed him and said she would be late.
Then Okoye turns to Hannah and asks, in a gentle voice, whether her sister's marriage was a happy one. Hannah opens her mouth to say yes, and finds that she honestly cannot tell.
Hannah explains that last Christmas she and Isla quarrelled about Isla's job. They said hurtful things, and then neither of them wrote or telephoned until the letter came.
By noon fifty volunteers have gathered on the quay to search the shore. Alma Finch, who runs the harbour cafe, pours tea from a huge steel pot and presses a mug into Hannah's hands.
In the afternoon a volunteer calls out from the sea wall and holds up a red scarf. Hannah feels her legs go weak, because she knitted that scarf herself, years ago, as a birthday present.

The sea rescue team searches the rocks below the wall until the tide comes in, and finds nothing. Owen tells Okoye that Isla wore the scarf on Friday morning, and the inspector does not say what she is thinking.
That evening the mayor announces that the Lantern Festival will be postponed by a fortnight. Men take down the paper lanterns in the square, and the lighthouse on Gull Island stays dark.
Late that night Hannah stands alone in the workshop doorway, beside a strip of police tape. She looks at the stopped clock and tells herself that a clock does not stop by itself.
On Sunday morning the Saltmere Gazette lands on the doormat with Isla's photograph on the front page. Larry Voss's article never says what it means, but it keeps mentioning the husband.
At the bakery, the whispering stops the moment Hannah walks through the door. Alma Finch is in the queue, and she says loudly that Owen Marlowe would not hurt a fly.
Hannah goes into Pryce Antiques, where a bell rings and a hundred clocks tick all at once. Gideon Pryce, silver-haired and smooth-voiced, says that Isla left the shop at five on Friday, as usual.
Pryce says Isla is the most gifted restorer he has ever employed. He offers to pay for posters, but he does not ask a single question about where she might be.
As Hannah passes the back stairs, a pale young assistant named Mabel Cray catches her sleeve. She whispers that Isla was very upset on Friday about some numbers in an old book.
Back in the workshop Hannah searches every corner the police might have missed. Taped beneath the bottom drawer of the bench she finds a small black notebook.
The notebook is filled with long numbers in Isla's neat handwriting, each beside a date. Hannah copies a page into her own notebook and hides the original in a teapot at home.
At Finch's Cafe Alma Finch says Isla had been worried lately. Last month she asked Alma what had happened to the old clock stolen from Saint Brannock's church.
That night Hannah lies awake thinking about long numbers and a stolen church clock. Downstairs she can hear Owen walking up and down the kitchen floor.
Hannah creeps to the top of the stairs and watches Owen through the kitchen door. He is staring into the dark garden, and she cannot read his face at all.
On Monday Inspector Okoye sits down at the kitchen table with a sheet of paper. She tells Owen that the bank shows a large sum of cash taken out of his account every month for six months.
Owen goes white and says nothing for a long time. At last he says only that he would never, ever hurt Isla, and that he cannot explain the money.
After the inspector has gone Hannah demands to know where the cash went. Owen begs her for a few more days of trust and promises that everything will become clear.
Mr Dunn, Owen's employer at the accountancy firm, telephones that afternoon. He says, kindly but firmly, that it would be better if Owen stayed away from the office for now.
By Tuesday morning reporters are standing outside the house on Marsh Street with cameras and notebooks. Larry Voss from the Gazette knocks on the door and asks for a word.
Larry lowers his voice and says that somebody sent him the tip about the bank cash. He will not say who, but the information came on Saturday, before even the police had it.
At dawn someone has painted WHERE IS ISLA on the garden gate in dripping letters. Owen scrubs it off with a bucket and brush before the neighbours can see it.
Over a silent breakfast Owen says that Isla has been quiet for weeks. She jumped whenever the telephone rang, and she looked, he thinks, like a person who was afraid of something.
Hannah telephones her school in the city and explains that she must stay in Saltmere. The head teacher is understanding and tells her to take as long as she needs.
At the police station Okoye asks Hannah about Isla's friends, her habits and her moods. Hannah tries to answer and slowly realises how little she knows about her sister's life now.
On Thursday old Mr Doyle calls to Hannah from his garden, where he is holding a small terrier. He tells her that on Friday evening he saw a green van with a pale stripe parked on Cobble Row.
Mr Doyle says a big man sat at the wheel with the engine running. The van drove away before it was properly dark, but he cannot say when exactly.
Hannah takes the story to Okoye, who says she has already logged the green van. But nobody has a number plate, and green vans are common in a fishing town.
Hannah walks to Anchor Lane to clear her head. She stops in front of her father's old workshop, now shuttered, with its faded name still visible above the door.
She remembers her father, Thomas Reed, with two little girls on stools beside his bench. He taught them how every clock works, and he loved timetables almost as much as clocks.
Hannah remembers the favourite game of their childhood, which they called Tick and Hide. The hider stopped a clock, and the time on its face told the seeker where to look.
Once, when Hannah was eight, Isla stopped the kitchen clock at a quarter past four. That was the time of the Thornby bus, and Hannah found her in the hay at Thornby Farm.
Hannah stands very still in the lane while a gull cries overhead. What if the stopped clock was not a mistake, and Isla meant it as a message for her sister alone?
Hannah hurries to the bus stop and the station to read the timetables. There is no bus at twenty to ten, and no train either.
She cannot work out the place yet, so she decides to look inside the clock itself. Isla, after all, always knew where to hide things.
At midnight Hannah slips out of the sleeping house with Owen's torch and creeps down Cobble Row. The police are finished here, and the street is silent.
Hannah shines the torch on the back of the tall clock. Around the screws she sees fresh scratches in the old varnish, as if somebody has opened the case recently.
Hannah unscrews the back panel and reaches behind the heavy brass weights. Her fingers touch a strip of tape, and under it there is a small brass key.
The key is stamped with a tiny pendulum, and it is far too small for a door. It must open a box, a drawer or a cupboard, and Hannah is determined to find which.
Hannah tries the key in every drawer of the workbench and every cupboard in the room. Not one of them has a lock that fits, and her hope begins to fade.
Hannah suddenly remembers something that their father always used to do. He hid his best tools and his spare money behind things that looked just like part of a wall.
Hannah starts to tap on the wooden panelling behind the tool shelves. Most of it gives a dull, solid sound, but one panel sounds hollow.
She pushes the panel sideways and it slides smoothly along a hidden groove. Behind it stands a narrow cabinet of dark wood, with a tiny keyhole in its door.
The key turns easily and the little door swings open. Inside are shelves of photographs, each showing a clock case and a small brass maker's plate.
Every photograph is labelled in Isla's handwriting with two long numbers. One of the numbers has been crossed out with a single firm line.
Hannah fetches the black notebook's copied page and compares it with the labels on the photographs. The crossed-out numbers match the notebook exactly, one after another.
At the bottom of the cabinet Hannah finds a yellow newspaper cutting from last April. The headline says that the turret clock of Saint Brannock's church has been stolen.
The cutting names the maker of the stolen clock and gives its number, because the church had listed it in its records. Hannah finds the very same number in Isla's notebook.
Slowly Hannah understands what all the long numbers mean. Isla had been tracing clocks that were stolen and then sold with false papers, and the trail led to her own employer.
At dawn Hannah tells Owen everything, and for once he looks fully awake. He jumps up and says that he is going straight to Pryce Antiques to make that man talk.
Hannah catches his sleeve and reminds him that they have no proof and that Pryce would only call the police. They agree to take everything to Inspector Okoye first.
Okoye studies the photographs for a long time without a word. Then she says that the evidence is interesting but it is not proof, and she warns Hannah not to act alone.
Okoye also scolds Hannah for hiding the black notebook for days. She promises, however, to read the file on the theft of the church clock herself.
Hannah visits Saint Brannock's, where the Reverend Joan Bright takes her up to the empty tower. Where the great clock once ticked there is only a bare iron frame.
The vicar says that Gideon Pryce came to see her a few weeks before the theft. He offered to buy the clock, to look after it, and she refused.
Next morning Hannah, ignoring the inspector's warning, walks down the narrow lane behind Pryce Antiques. She tells herself firmly that she will only look and will not go in.
Through a gap in the gate she sees a yard and a green van with a pale stripe along its side. A very big man in overalls is washing it slowly with a bucket.
The big man looks up and sees her eye at the gap. He stares for a long time without speaking, and then he slams the van door so hard that it echoes.
The back door opens and Mabel Cray hurries across the yard, very pale. She whispers that Hannah must go away and begs her not to come back.
Gideon Pryce stands at the back door with a gentle smile and invites Hannah in for a cup of tea. Against her better judgement, and with her heart beating fast, she accepts.
In his cluttered office Pryce pours tea and speaks sadly about poor Owen. He remarks that the money Owen has been taking from the bank must be a heavy worry.
Pryce smiles and tells Hannah that Isla was clever, but that clever people can be curious. He says it is sometimes wiser not to ask questions about old clocks.
Hannah thanks him for the tea and walks out through the shop, the bell ringing behind her. She is shaking, but she is certain of one thing, which is that Pryce is afraid.
Outside, in the lane, Hannah quickly writes part of the van's number plate on her hand. She managed to see three letters and two numbers through the gate.
Okoye checks the number and finds that the van belongs to Pryce Antiques. Pryce says his driver delivered a clock to Isla's workshop at dusk, which does not match what he told Hannah.
That night Hannah dozes on the sofa and wakes with a jolt. Through the front window she sees a small torch beam moving at the end of Cobble Row.
Hannah shakes Owen awake and they run down the lane together in their coats. When they reach the workshop the door has been forced, and the torch beam is gone.
Inside, the hidden panel has been dragged aside and the narrow cabinet stands open and bare. Every photograph and cutting has disappeared, and only a few scraps of tape remain.

Suddenly she understands the old game of her childhood. The time on the clock is a timetable, and the place it names is Gull Island, where the last boat sails.
Hannah runs all the way back to Marsh Street and stops in the hall. The empty hook that she noticed on the first morning is where Isla's grey raincoat always hangs.
Hannah tells Owen everything she has worked out, and he goes pale. He says that Isla's old teacher, Miss Agnes Penhale, lives in a little cottage beside the lighthouse on Gull Island.

At the top of the hill the lighthouse rises white with its red band, and beside it stands a small cottage. A thread of smoke is rising from the chimney.

A door opens at the back of the room, and a thin young woman stands in it. Her hair has been cut very short, but it is Isla, and she is alive.
Owen crosses the room in two strides and takes his wife in his arms. He holds her so tightly that neither of them can speak, while Hannah laughs and weeps at the same moment.
At last Isla turns to her sister and whispers, “You found my clock.” Hannah answers through her tears, “You stopped it,” and then they hold each other tightly.

Owen tells Isla that the whole town has suspected him of harming her. Isla, who has had no news on the island, is horrified, and she begins to shake.
Miss Penhale decides that everyone has had enough excitement for the moment. She puts the kettle on the stove and announces that tea comes before explanations.
They all sit down round the table with cups of hot tea, and Owen will not let go of Isla's hand. Isla takes a deep breath and says that she will begin with Gideon Pryce.
Isla says that about two months ago she noticed something odd on a clock that had come into Pryce's workshop. The number stamped on its plate was sharper and newer than the rest of the brass.

Slowly Isla understands what Pryce has been doing for years. He removes the genuine maker's plates, stamps new ones with different numbers and writes false papers to match.
One day Pryce sends Isla to fetch a spring from his barn at Thornby. Under some blankets she finds Saint Brannock's stolen turret clock, with its old plate still screwed on.
Isla unscrews the brass plate with a pocket screwdriver and slips it into her bag. A few days later, while Pryce is at lunch, she copies his account book page by page.
On Friday at dusk Pryce discovers that the plate is missing and comes to Isla's workshop with Rufus and the van. He tells her softly that careful hands can break as easily as old clocks.
Isla pretends, with a perfectly calm face, to agree with him. She tells Pryce that she will hand over the plate on Monday, and he leaves, but she knows that he will not wait.
Isla knows that she must disappear at once, so she stops the tall clock at twenty to ten. She leaves her phone and her scarf behind and boards the last boat to Gull Island.
Isla says she told nobody because Owen is honest and bad at lying, and Pryce was watching them all. She had invited Hannah to the festival because only Hannah would understand the clock.
Isla opens her bag and takes out two things wrapped in flannel. One is the brass maker's plate from the church clock, and the other is a biscuit tin full of copied papers.
Meanwhile in Saltmere Mabel Cray hurries to Pryce and tells him that Hannah was asking questions at the ferry shed. Pryce, who has been losing patience, begins to smile.
Pryce pays Rufus a fistful of banknotes, and the two men hurry to Thornby cove. There they hire a small fishing boat, the Gannet, and set out across the water.
On the island Owen begs Isla to come home with them at once. She says she wants to give the proof to Inspector Okoye first, because without it nobody will believe her.

Miss Penhale takes the visitors to the garden and points at the lighthouse. She tells them that its lamp is lit only on festival eves, and that this year it is sleeping because the festival has been postponed.
On the island the telephone signal is poor, so Owen climbs the hill behind the cottage. At the top he reaches Okoye, who says that the police launch will cross by nightfall.
In the afternoon Hannah and Isla walk out to the cliff and sit on the grass. For the first time in a year they talk about their quarrel, quietly and honestly.

Isla admits that she took the job with Pryce because the family needed money after their father died. The work spoiled when she saw what he was doing, and Hannah says she is sorry for her harsh words.
As the light begins to fade, Owen cooks supper on Miss Penhale's old stove. Suddenly everyone hears an engine, low and steady, somewhere out on the water.
Miss Penhale goes to the window and looks down toward the jetty. A small fishing boat has tied up there, and two men are standing on its deck.
Soon there is a knock at the blue door, firm and polite. Nobody moves until Isla stands up, and when she opens the door Gideon Pryce says, “Good evening, Isla.”
Pryce stands in the doorway with a charming smile, and the big man Rufus waits behind him in the garden. He says that he has come a long way to ask, politely, for the plate.
Isla stays remarkably calm and polite, even now that Pryce is standing in her room. She puts the plate and tin on the sideboard and asks him to sit, because she wants to hear how he did it.
While Pryce settles in the armchair, Hannah slips into the kitchen and whispers an idea to Miss Penhale. The old woman nods and points to the lighthouse key that hangs by the back door.
Isla asks one clever question after another about clocks, and Pryce, who loves to boast, begins to talk. He says that the church clock was the finest piece he has ever handled.
Hannah takes the heavy iron key from its hook and eases open the back door. Behind her she can hear Isla's voice, steady and curious, and Pryce's pleased answers.
Hannah runs across the moor toward the lighthouse, which stands pale against the darkening sky. The wind snatches at her coat, and the heather tugs at her ankles.
The key turns in the old lock, and Hannah goes in. She climbs the spiral stairs in the dark, counting each step aloud, as she did as a child.
In the lantern room the old lamp stands dark inside its huge glass lens. By the wall is a switch behind a small pane of glass, exactly as Miss Penhale once showed her.
Without waiting a second longer, Hannah throws the heavy switch down. The lamp hums and wakes, and then a great white beam sweeps out over the dark water.
On the mainland Inspector Okoye sees the beam from the quay and goes very still. She knows that the lamp burns only on festival nights, and she calls for the police launch.
In the cottage a bar of white light slides across the window and across Pryce's face. He stops talking in the middle of a word and slowly understands what it means.
Pryce leaps up, snatches the biscuit tin and the plate from the sideboard and runs for the door. In the garden he shouts for Rufus, and they race together toward the jetty.
Owen runs out after them, shouting for them to stop. Miss Penhale hurries to the garden gate and shuts it firmly in front of Rufus, who has to climb over the wall.
At the top of the tower Hannah hears shouting far below, and she leaves the lamp burning and rushes down the stairs. She almost falls twice, but she does not stop.
Owen is faster than anyone expects, and he reaches the jetty first. He stands in the middle of the narrow stone causeway with his arms spread wide, blocking the way to the boat.
Pryce arrives panting, clutching the tin to his chest. He orders Owen to step aside, and Owen answers in a clear steady voice, “No.”
Rufus has climbed down into the Gannet, but he looks up and sees a blue flashing light far out on the water. It is the police launch, and he sits down in the boat and puts his hands on his knees.
Pryce lunges at Owen to push past him, but his smooth shoes slip on the wet boards. The tin flies from his arms, and Owen puts his foot on it before it can fall into the sea.
The police launch roars in with its engines throbbing, and a searchlight sweeps the jetty. Everyone is lit up like actors on a stage, and nobody can run any longer.
Inspector Okoye steps ashore, calm as ever, and looks down at Pryce. She arrests Gideon Pryce, and Owen hands her the tin with the brass plate inside.
That night in Miss Penhale's cottage Okoye takes statements from everyone. Isla hands over the copied account book from the biscuit tin, and Okoye reads it page by page.
Okoye tells Isla sternly that she wasted a great deal of police time, but that she will not be charged. Then she admits that Isla was right, and that she herself was slow.
At dawn the police launch brings everyone back to Saltmere, with Pryce and Rufus under guard. On the steps of the police station Mabel Cray is waiting, white-faced and shivering.
Mabel tells Okoye that she helped change the plates and write the false papers. She also told Pryce about the ferryman, and she says that she is sorry and will give evidence.
With the brass plate and Mabel's confession in hand, Okoye goes to the magistrate. This time she comes away with a signed warrant to search the barn at Thornby.
The police cut off the new padlock and swing the big doors wide. In the dim light, under a heap of grey blankets, stands the great turret clock of Saint Brannock's.
Behind the great clock there are wooden crates, each one full of old clocks with new brass plates. In a drawer there is also an invoice from a foreign buyer, dated for Monday.
The Reverend Joan Bright is brought to the barn, and she weeps when she sees the old clock. Isla fits the brass plate into its place on the frame, and it fits perfectly.
The next Saltmere Gazette has a new front page. Its headline says that the husband is cleared and the missing wife is safe, and Larry Voss has written a short, honest apology.
All day neighbours knock on the door at Marsh Street with pies, flowers and awkward apologies. Owen forgives them with a kind smile, though Hannah forgives rather more slowly.
At home on Marsh Street the clocks are silent, because nobody has wound them. Isla goes through the house winding each one, and last of all she restarts the tall clock from the workshop.
Owen takes the heavy brass key from his pocket and puts it in Isla's hand. He tells her that it opens her father's old workshop on Anchor Lane, which is hers.
Together they unlock the door and walk into the old workshop, with dust floating in the light. On the doorframe Isla finds her initials, carved long ago with a penknife.
Hannah tells them that she has applied for a teaching job at the primary school in Saltmere. She says that she would like to be nearer her sister, and Isla hugs her.
At sunrise the sisters sit on the sea wall with the red scarf between them. They promise each other that, whatever happens, neither of them will keep a secret from the other again.
Volunteers from all over the town carry the turret clock up to Saint Brannock's. With the vicar watching, and Isla giving orders, they lift it through the tower door and into its place.
At last Isla stands before the great clock in the tower and takes hold of the pendulum. She gives it a gentle push, and for the first time since April the clock begins to tick.
On the evening of the postponed festival the whole town gathers at the harbour. Thousands of paper lanterns glow along the quay, and children carry them on sticks.
Out on Gull Island Miss Penhale pulls the switch, as she has done for many years. The great lamp wakes, and its beam sweeps slowly across the water and over the lanterns of the harbour.
At ten o'clock exactly the great clock in the tower of Saint Brannock's begins to strike. Its deep notes roll out over the harbour, and Hannah, Isla and Owen listen to every one.

Isla wrote of the festival, of the spare room and of how much she hoped Hannah would come, and she did not mention the quarrel once. It was a lovely letter, but something in its careful, polished phrasing had troubled Hannah since the morning it arrived.

The train drew in beside the harbour just as dusk was settling, and along the quay men on ladders were threading paper lanterns between the lamp posts. Out across the water Gull Island lay low and black, its lighthouse unlit, for by old custom the great lamp would burn only on the night of the festival. Hannah breathed in salt and woodsmoke and felt, to her own surprise, a small tug of homesickness for a town she had left years before.

Her brother-in-law was waiting beside the ticket office, a neat, quiet man in a buttoned coat who always seemed to be thinking about something else. He kissed her cheek, took her bag with his usual courtesy and explained that Isla was finishing a repair at her workshop and would join them presently. His smile came a moment too late, and the shadows beneath his eyes suggested that he had not slept properly for days.

They walked up from the harbour through narrow streets strung with unlit lanterns, and passed the bright window of Pryce Antiques, where rows of polished clocks stood in the glow like well-behaved children. Isla had worked there for nearly two years, restoring the old mechanisms that Gideon Pryce sold to collectors. When Hannah asked how the job was going, Owen only said that Isla had been staying late, and he changed the subject to the weather.

The house on Marsh Street was crowded with clocks, on the stairs, along the mantelpiece and even in the bathroom, and each one ticked at a slightly different speed, so that the whole building seemed to murmur. Upstairs the spare room had been prepared with clean sheets, a folded towel and a jug of yellow flowers that had plainly been picked that very morning. Hannah touched a petal and thought how very like Isla it was to make a welcome without being there to see it.

A fish pie stood on the kitchen table beneath a cloth, with three plates, three forks and a bottle of lemonade laid out beside it, exactly as though Isla had stepped away for a minute. They waited for an hour, making the careful small talk of people who do not want to say what they are thinking. Owen kept glancing at the door, and each time he looked, the pie cooled a little more.

At last Owen took out his own phone and rang his wife's number, and somewhere in the kitchen a faint buzzing began. Hannah followed the sound to the drawer beside the sink and found Isla's phone lying among the spoons and tea towels, its screen glowing with her husband's name. Nobody leaves home without a phone by accident on the evening before a festival, and the same thought passed silently between them.

Owen snatched a torch from the hook in the hall, and the two of them hurried out into the dark and down the cobbled slope of Cobble Row, where Isla kept her own small workshop. Hannah's heart was beating in her ears, and every unlit lantern they passed swung in the wind like a question. The workshop door stood a hand's width open, and behind it a single yellow lamp was burning.

Inside, everything was orderly: the tools hung in their outlines on the wall, and a carriage clock lay half-mended beneath the lamp as if its mender had only paused for a breath. In the corner the tall clock stood absolutely silent, its pendulum hanging still and its hands fixed at twenty to ten. Of Isla there was no sign at all, and Hannah, who had grown up among clocks, knew that a good clock does not simply stop.

At midnight Owen telephoned the police, and a weary voice on the line promised that an officer would call in the morning, which was not the comfort he had hoped for. Hannah lay awake in the spare room with the yellow flowers breathing their scent into the dark, listening to thirty clocks ticking out of step. Somewhere beneath all that noise she kept hearing the one silence, the clock in the workshop that had stopped at twenty to ten.

Before anyone else was awake Hannah searched the house as gently as she could, opening drawers and lifting cushions with the guilty care of a person looking through a sister's life. Isla's passport lay in its usual place, her purse and bank cards were in the kitchen, and her good blue coat hung by the door. Only one hook in the hall was bare, but Hannah, thinking of other things, did not notice it enough to ask what had hung there.

Inspector Dana Okoye arrived at nine o'clock with a young constable called Priya Nair, and she carried herself with the unhurried calm of a person who has seen a great many worried families. Before she accepted a cup of tea she asked to be taken to the workshop, and she walked round it twice without touching anything. She stood longest in front of the tall clock, her head tilted, as though it were a witness that had decided not to talk.

At the kitchen table Okoye opened a small notebook and asked Owen to describe, as exactly as he could, the last time he had seen his wife. He told her that they had breakfasted together on Friday, that Isla had been unusually quiet, and that she had kissed him at the door and promised to be home for supper. His voice cracked on the word supper, and Okoye wrote something down and waited without hurrying him.

Then Okoye turned to Hannah and asked, in a perfectly neutral voice, whether her sister's marriage had been a happy one. Hannah opened her mouth to say yes, as loyalty required, and discovered to her dismay that she had no real knowledge on which to base the answer. She had not seen the couple for a year, and she said so, and the admission sat on the table between them like an extra cup.

Hannah told the story slowly and without excuses, because it did not reflect well on her. At Christmas a year earlier she had accused Isla of selling her talent to Gideon Pryce and giving up on their late father's dream of a workshop of their own, and Isla had answered with words just as sharp. After that neither sister had written or telephoned, until the cheerful letter had arrived out of a clear sky.

By noon some fifty volunteers in boots and waterproofs had gathered on the quay, drawn by the particular loyalty that a small town reserves for a missing neighbour. Alma Finch, who ran the cafe by the harbour, was pouring tea from an enormous steel pot and pressing a mug into every hand, including Hannah's. Her kindness was so plain and so sudden that Hannah felt her eyes sting, and had to look hard at the water until the feeling passed.

In the middle of the afternoon a volunteer shouted from the far end of the sea wall and held up something bright, a long scarf of knitted red wool, folded neatly and weighted down with a stone. Hannah's legs went weak beneath her, because she knew every stitch of it, having made it herself years ago for Isla's birthday, with a dropped stitch near one end that nobody else would ever have noticed. She told the inspector so in a voice she hardly recognised, and then she had to sit down on the cold stones of the quay.

The coastguard searched the rocks and the shallows below the wall until the incoming tide drove them back, and the sea, which might have given something up, gave nothing. Owen confirmed to Okoye that Isla had worn the red scarf when she left the house on Friday morning, and his face had the stunned, grey look of a man who is being asked to believe the worst. All around the square men on ladders unhooked the paper lanterns one by one, and folded them away like the wings of tired birds. Far out across the water the lighthouse on Gull Island remained dark, as though the whole coast were holding its breath.

Late that night, when the house had finally gone quiet, Hannah walked back down Cobble Row and stood alone in the doorway of the workshop, beside a fluttering strip of police tape. The tall clock loomed in the corner, motionless, with its hands still pointing to twenty to ten. She had grown up in her father's shop, where every stopped clock had a reason, and she became quite certain that this one had been stopped on purpose.

On Sunday morning the Saltmere Gazette landed on the doormat with a photograph of Isla beneath a headline in thick black type. The article, signed by a reporter called Larry Voss, never quite accused anyone of anything, yet it mentioned the husband in nearly every paragraph and used the word questioned twice. Owen read it standing in the hall, folded it very small and put it in the bin without a word.

At the bakery the whispering stopped the instant Hannah walked in, and a dozen faces turned politely toward the shelves of bread. She had never been so aware of her own footsteps, or of how loud a bakery bell can sound. Alma Finch, who was waiting for her rolls, declared in a carrying voice that Owen Marlowe wouldn't hurt a fly, and that anyone who thought otherwise could say so to her face.

A bell tinkled as Hannah pushed open the door of Pryce Antiques, and a hundred clocks seemed to turn their faces toward her. Gideon Pryce came forward from the back of the shop, silver-haired, soft-voiced and beautifully dressed, with his hands spread in sympathy. He told her that Isla had left the shop at five o'clock on Friday as she always did, that she had seemed perfectly well and that he was desperately sorry.

Pryce spoke warmly of Isla's gift, which he described as the finest he had ever employed, and he pressed a folded banknote into Hannah's hand to help pay for missing-person posters. It was generously done, and Hannah thanked him, but on her way to the door she realised that he had not asked one question. He had not wondered aloud where Isla might have gone, or who might have seen her, or whether there was any news.

As Hannah passed the foot of the back stairs a pale young woman in a grey cardigan caught at her sleeve, glanced over her shoulder and spoke in a breathless whisper. Her name was Mabel Cray, and she worked in the shop as Mr Pryce's young assistant, though she looked scarcely old enough to have left school. She said that on Friday afternoon Isla had been badly upset about some numbers in an old book, and then, before Hannah could ask a single question, she hurried away up the stairs.

Back in the workshop Hannah searched every corner that a busy police officer might have overlooked, and she did it as Isla would have, by thinking about where a clockmaker hides a thing. Beneath the lowest drawer of the workbench, held up with a long strip of tape, she found a small black notebook with a worn cover. It had clearly been put there in a hurry, and by somebody who wanted it found only by the right person.

The little notebook was filled from cover to cover with long numbers in Isla's neat handwriting, each followed by a date and a pair of letters that meant nothing to Hannah. She copied a page into her own notebook, in case something happened to the original, and then she carried the black one home and hid it in the back of the dresser, inside a teapot that nobody ever used. She did not know yet whether she was protecting evidence or protecting her sister.

At Finch's Cafe, over a mug of tea she had not asked for, Alma Finch said that Isla had seemed worried for weeks, though she would not say why. Only last month she had stopped at the counter and asked, quite out of nowhere, whether anyone had ever found out what became of the great clock stolen from the tower of Saint Brannock's. Alma had told her that the police had given up, and Isla had gone very quiet.

That night Hannah lay awake turning two facts over in her mind like coins, the long numbers in her sister's notebook and the tower clock stolen from Saint Brannock's. They did not seem to belong together, and yet something in her memory kept insisting that they did. Downstairs the kitchen floorboards creaked as Owen paced from the stove to the window and back again, hour after hour.

Hannah crept to the top of the stairs and watched through the banisters as Owen stood motionless at the kitchen window, staring out at the black garden. He did not look like a guilty man, and he did not look like an innocent one either; he looked like a man carrying something heavy that he had promised not to put down. She went back to bed wondering, uneasily, what her brother-in-law was keeping from her.

Then she asked him, quite gently and without taking her eyes from his face, where all that money had gone.

Owen went white, and for a long time the only sound in the room was the ticking of the clocks. When at last he spoke, it was to say, very quietly, that he would never in his life hurt Isla, and that he was not able to explain the money.
