When the inspector had gone, Hannah rounded on him in the kitchen and demanded to know where the money had gone, because her sister was missing and there was no room for secrets. Owen only held up his hands and begged her for a few more days of trust, swearing that when the time came everything would make sense. Hannah wanted desperately to believe him, but belief, she found, was not something that could be ordered like a cup of tea.

That afternoon the telephone rang, and it was Mr Dunn, the senior partner at the accountancy firm where Owen had worked for eleven years. He was kind and he was embarrassed, and he said that in the circumstances, and with the newspapers as they were, it might be wiser for Owen to stay away from the office for a while. Owen thanked him politely, put down the receiver and stood looking at it for a long time.

By Tuesday morning a small crowd of reporters had gathered outside the house on Marsh Street, with cameras, notebooks and the patient look of people who have sensed a story. Larry Voss from the Gazette, a thin man with an eager face and a crumpled raincoat, walked up the path and knocked on the door as though he were a visiting relative. Hannah opened it just wide enough to tell him that nobody was giving interviews.

Larry lowered his voice and, rather to Hannah's surprise, admitted that he had not found out about the cash for himself. Someone had telephoned the newspaper on Saturday afternoon and passed on the information, he said, and he would not name the caller, but the tip had arrived before the police themselves had seen the bank's records. Hannah closed the door slowly and stood in the hall for some time, wondering who could possibly have known so much so soon.

Early on Wednesday, before the street was properly awake, somebody crept up to the house and painted three dripping words across the garden gate, WHERE IS ISLA. Hannah found Owen out there at first light with a bucket and a scrubbing brush, working at the letters with a grim, patient energy. He did not say anything, and she did not either, and she picked up a cloth and began to help him.

Over a silent breakfast Owen finally admitted something that he had not said to the police. For weeks Isla had been quieter than usual, sleeping badly and starting at every ring of the telephone, and he had put it down to overwork, though he now believed she had been afraid. It was the first thing he had told Hannah that made her feel they were on the same side.

Hannah walked up and down the back garden with her telephone pressed to her ear and explained to the head teacher at her school in the city that she would not be coming back on Monday. The woman was sympathetic and practical, and she told Hannah to take as long as she needed, and that the class would manage. When Hannah put the telephone away, the decision felt strangely light, as though she had finally stopped pretending she might leave.

At the police station Okoye pulled out a clean sheet of paper and asked Hannah to list Isla's friends, her habits, her favourite places and her recent moods. Hannah began confidently, with the people from their childhood, and then trailed off as she understood that she knew almost nothing about the person her sister had become. It was a bitter discovery, and the inspector, to her credit, did not remark on it, and simply slid a card across the desk.

On Thursday morning old Mr Doyle, who lived next door to the workshop, beckoned Hannah over to his hedge with a trembling finger, his small terrier tucked under one arm. He had been turning something over in his mind, he said, and he had mentioned it to the young constable, who had written nothing down. On Friday at dusk he had seen a green van with a pale stripe along its side parked right outside the workshop door.

Mr Doyle was quite sure of the details, for he had nothing to do in the evenings but watch the lane from his window. A big man had sat at the wheel the whole time with the engine running, he said, never getting out, never switching on a light, and the van had driven off down the hill before it was properly dark. He had not seen who went into the workshop, and he could not swear to the hour, which he said was the great pity.

Hannah carried the story to Okoye, who listened attentively and then said, without any unkindness, that she had already logged the van. Nobody had seen its number plate, she explained, and in a town of fishermen and builders and delivery drivers there were a great many green vans with stripes. It was not nothing, she added, but it was not yet a lead, and she asked Hannah to keep it to herself.

To clear her head Hannah walked the length of Anchor Lane, past the net lofts and the chandler's, until she came to the narrow shuttered shop where her father had worked for forty years. The paint on the door had faded and the window was grey with salt, but above it the old sign was still just legible, REED, CLOCKMAKER. She laid a hand against the cold wood of the shutter and let the memories come.

She remembered her father, Thomas Reed, bent over his bench with his spectacles pushed up onto his forehead, while two small girls perched on stools and watched the brass wheels turn. He had taught them how a clock was put together, and how to listen to it, and also, for reasons that had never been clear, how to read a timetable. He believed that a time was never just a number, and that every one of them led somewhere.

Hannah suddenly remembered the game that the sisters had played for years, which they called Tick and Hide. The hider would slip away and stop a clock at a particular time, and the seeker, by thinking of a bus or a train that left at that hour, would work out the place where the hider was waiting. It had been a secret language between the two of them, and nobody else had ever understood it.

One summer, when Hannah was eight and Isla eleven, Isla stopped the kitchen clock at a quarter past four and vanished, and Hannah had spent a tearful hour before she thought of the timetable on the wall. A quarter past four was the Thornby bus, and she had run all the way to the stop, and from there to Thornby Farm, where Isla was lying giggling in the hay. That memory made Hannah's heart thump, for it was exactly the kind of thing her sister would do again.

Hannah stood very still in the lane while a gull cried overhead, and a thought arrived that she could not push away. What if the stopped clock in the workshop was not an accident, or a sign of struggle, but a message, the old game played again by a woman who trusted that only one person in the world would understand it? The idea was so extraordinary and so likely that she felt dizzy, and had to steady herself against the cold wall of her father's shop.

Hannah hurried to the bus stop on the square, and then to the railway station, and read both timetables from top to bottom with her finger on the glass. No bus left Saltmere at twenty to ten in the evening, and no train departed then either, and she walked away baffled. Something was clearly wrong with her reading of the clue, or she had missed some part of it that was still waiting to be found.

She could not yet solve the puzzle of the time, but she could examine the clock itself, and she knew that Isla had never in her life hidden anything in a place where it would be easy to find. Hannah decided that she would return to the workshop that very night, when the street was quiet and Mr Doyle's window was dark. A good clockmaker, her father used to say, never trusts the face of a clock until he has looked inside the case.

At midnight, with the whole house asleep, Hannah took Owen's torch from the hook, eased the front door shut behind her and crept down Cobble Row in her softest shoes. The police had finished with the workshop, the tape had been pulled away, and the street lay silent under a thin wash of moonlight. Even so, she kept looking over her shoulder as though the shadows might have opinions.

She shone the torch over the tall clock, slowly, from the plinth to the hood, and at the back of the case her beam caught something small. Around each brass screw there were fine fresh scratches in the old varnish, the kind a screwdriver leaves when it has been used in a hurry. Somebody had opened this case recently, and Hannah felt quite sure that she knew exactly who it had been.

With her heart thudding Hannah unscrewed the back of the case and slipped her hand behind the heavy brass weights, feeling along the dusty wood. Her fingertips met a strip of sticky tape, and beneath it, pressed flat against the panel, lay a small brass key. It belonged to no part of the clock, and its smooth, hand-warmed look suggested that it had been handled many times.

Under the torch the little key proved to be stamped with the tiniest of pendulums, a mark that Hannah had last seen on a box of tools in her father's shop. It was much too small for any door in the building, so it must open something compact, a drawer or a case or a cupboard of some kind. She closed her fingers over it and felt the old thrill of a puzzle half solved.

She tried the key in every drawer of the workbench, then in the tool chest, the cupboard under the window and the narrow box where Isla kept her spare springs. Not one of them took it, and the longer she worked, the louder the silence of the room seemed to grow. At last she sat back on her heels, tired and a little foolish, and tried to think like her sister.

In the hush of the workshop she remembered one of her father's quiet eccentricities. Thomas Reed had never trusted a safe, because any thief would go straight to it, and instead he used to hide his best tools and his emergency money behind objects that looked exactly like part of the building. Isla had loved that trick as a child, and Hannah could easily believe that she had grown up to use it.

She began to knock gently on the wooden panelling that ran behind the shelves, working along it from one end to the other with the knuckle of her forefinger. Most of the boards answered with a dull and solid thud, but one panel near the corner replied with a different note, light and hollow, like a drum with nothing inside. Hannah held her breath, laid the torch down on the bench and pressed her palm flat against that one board.

The panel resisted for a moment and then slid sideways along a groove that had been smoothly oiled, and behind it, set into the thickness of the wall, stood a narrow cabinet of dark wood. Its door was barely wider than a book, and in the centre, small and neat, was a keyhole. Hannah thought of all the times she had stood in this room without seeing it, and of everything else she might be failing to see.

The key slid in and turned with a soft click, and the narrow door swung open on four shelves crowded with neat stacks of photographs. Each one showed a clock, a tall case or a mantel clock or a bracket clock, and beside it a close view of the small brass plate on which a maker's name and number are stamped. Hannah drew out the first photograph and held it under the torch with fingers that were not quite steady.

Every photograph had been labelled on the back in Isla's small upright handwriting, with a date and two long numbers, the first of which had been struck through with a single firm line. Hannah turned over one after another and the pattern repeated exactly, a crossed-out number and a fresh one, as though two different histories had been written for each of the clocks. Something here was very wrong, and Isla had taken enormous trouble to record it.

She hurried home through the sleeping lanes, fetched her copy of the notebook page from its hiding place and laid it out beside the photographs on the kitchen table. The crossed-out numbers on the photographs matched the numbers in the notebook exactly, one after another, down the whole page. It was no longer possible to believe that Isla had been merely keeping a hobby.

At the very bottom of the cabinet, beneath the last stack of photographs, lay a yellowed newspaper cutting dated the previous April. The headline reported that the great turret clock of Saint Brannock's church had been stolen from its tower in the night, by thieves who had known exactly which bolts to loosen. Beside it, in Isla's handwriting, was a single line: This is where it began.

The cutting named the maker of the stolen clock, a Victorian firm from the north, and quoted its serial number from the church's own records. Hannah ran her finger down the page of the black notebook until she found the same long string of digits, set down by Isla several weeks before, with a small star beside it. The two numbers might as well have been shouting at each other across the table.

Slowly, as one understands a language after hearing it for a long while, Hannah understood the pattern. Old clocks were being stolen, their true numbers were being covered by false ones, and they were being sold to collectors with papers that invented an innocent past, while the trail seemed to run through the shop where Isla worked. Her sister had found all of this out by herself, and she had been gathering proof alone and in secret.

At dawn Hannah told Owen everything, the notebook, the key, the cabinet and the stolen church clock, and for the first time that week his tired face came fully awake. He jumped up from his chair so quickly that it fell over behind him, and declared that he was going straight to Pryce Antiques to make the man talk. It was the nearest Hannah had ever seen the gentle accountant come to anything resembling violence.

Hannah caught his sleeve and held on, reminding him that all they had was a handful of photographs and some numbers, and that if he stormed into the shop Pryce would simply telephone the police and describe a threatening husband. Slowly, with a great shuddering breath, Owen sat down again and set the fallen chair back on its legs, and the anger drained out of him. They agreed to take every scrap of evidence to Inspector Okoye before they did anything else.

Inspector Okoye spread the photographs across her desk and studied them for a long time without speaking, turning each one so that the light fell across the brass plates. At last she said that it was interesting, genuinely interesting, but that it was not yet proof of anything a court would accept, since copies and notes could be explained away. She added, with real seriousness, that Hannah must not go looking for Pryce by herself.

Okoye also told Hannah, quite sharply, that hiding the black notebook for days had been foolish and might have cost the police valuable time, and Hannah took the reproach with a lowered head. Then the inspector's face softened a little, and she promised that she would pull out the old file on the church theft and read it again that very afternoon. It was not much, but after so many days of nothing it felt like the first real beginning.

That afternoon Hannah walked up the hill to Saint Brannock's, where the Reverend Joan Bright, a brisk woman in a cardigan, led her up the narrow stairs of the tower. The chamber at the top was bare and cold and full of pigeons, and where the great turret clock had once ticked there remained only a rusted iron frame and four empty bolt holes. The vicar said that the church had never felt the same since the silence began.

As they descended, the vicar remembered something that she had told the police at the time, though they had not seemed to think it important. A few weeks before the theft Mr Pryce had called at the vicarage and kindly offered to buy the turret clock, supposedly to keep it safe, and she had refused. Hannah stopped on the stair and gripped the rope handrail, because the pieces were beginning to click.

The next morning, against all the inspector's advice and a good deal of her own sense, Hannah walked down the narrow lane that ran behind the shops of Harbour Street. She told herself that she would only look, and that a person is allowed to walk down a public lane, and that nobody could possibly object. Her feet carried her on, past the dustbins and a sleeping cat, to the high gate of Pryce Antiques.

Through a gap between the planks of the gate she saw a cobbled yard, and in the middle of it a green van with a pale stripe along its flank. A very big man in overalls, whom she took to be Rufus Dray, was washing it slowly and thoroughly with a bucket and a long-handled brush. She noticed that he was scrubbing the same patch of the wheel arch for the third time.

The big man looked up, as if some animal sense had warned him, and his eyes met hers through the gap in the planks. He neither spoke nor moved for what seemed a very long time, and then he turned, climbed into the van and slammed the door so hard that the whole yard rang. Hannah took a step backward, and realised that she had been holding her breath.

The back door of the shop flew open and Mabel Cray came hurrying across the cobbles, her grey cardigan clutched about her and her face as white as milk. She whispered that Hannah must go away at once, that it was not safe, and that for pity's sake she must not come back. Before Hannah could ask what she meant, a quiet voice spoke from the doorway.

Gideon Pryce stood in the doorway with his silver head slightly tilted and an expression of perfect hospitality, and he asked Hannah whether she would care to come in for a cup of tea. Every sensible instinct told her to refuse, but a stronger instinct, the wish to look into the man's face while he talked, made her nod and follow him inside. Mabel melted away through the yard without a sound, and the heavy door closed softly behind the two of them.

In his panelled office, where a dozen clocks ticked softly on the walls, Pryce poured the tea with a steady hand and spoke sorrowfully about poor Owen. It must be a terrible burden, he murmured, to have all that cash drawn from the bank and no explanation for it. Hannah looked at her cup and understood that the figures had been mentioned to the newspaper and to nobody else, so how could Pryce know?

Pryce stirred his tea with a tiny silver spoon and observed, in the gentlest possible voice, that Isla had been a clever woman, and that cleverness was often accompanied by curiosity. It was sometimes wiser, he said, not to ask too many questions about old clocks, because the answers were so rarely welcome. His smile never altered, and that, to Hannah, was the most frightening thing of all.

Hannah thanked him for the tea in a voice that she hoped sounded steady, and walked out through the shop with the bell tinkling behind her and a hundred clocks watching her go. Her knees were trembling and her mouth was dry, yet beneath the fear she felt a hard bright certainty. A man who goes to such trouble to frighten a visitor is a man with something terrible to lose.

Outside, in the lane, Hannah took a pen from her bag and wrote on the back of her hand the part of the number plate that she had managed to see through the gate. It was only three letters and two numbers, but it was more than anyone else had, and she held it like a precious thing all the way to the police station. Her hand was still trembling as she wrote, and she had to press hard on the pen to make the figures clear.

Okoye checked the partial number against her records and found that the van was registered to Pryce Antiques. When she had questioned Pryce, he had calmly explained that his driver had delivered a clock to Isla's workshop at about six on Friday evening, a detail that he had somehow forgotten to mention earlier. It could not be reconciled with his claim that Isla had left the shop at five, and the inspector's eyes were very bright.

That night Hannah, too restless for bed, dozed on the sofa in the front room with a blanket round her knees, and woke with a jolt at some small hour of the morning. Through the window and across the dark roofs she could see, at the end of Cobble Row, a thin beam of torchlight moving slowly back and forth inside Isla's workshop. Nobody on earth had any right to be in that place at such an hour of the night.

She shook Owen awake and they ran down the cobbled lane together, buttoning their coats as they went, with the wind loud in their ears. By the time they reached the workshop the torch beam had vanished, and the door hung open on a splintered frame, its lock hanging by one screw. Whoever had been there had gone, and had not troubled to be quiet about it.

Inside, the hidden panel had been wrenched aside, and the narrow cabinet stood open and bare, like a mouth that had been silenced. Every photograph and every cutting had vanished, and nothing remained of Isla's careful record except a few scraps of tape and the faint ghost of a ring where a stack had stood. Hannah felt sick, for she understood that she had been followed, or that someone had guessed.

In the alley behind the workshop a broad tyre mark was printed deeply in the damp earth, with a dark smear of oil beside it, and the air still smelled of hot metal. Far down the hill an engine was dying away into the night, too distant to be followed and too late to be stopped. Owen stood with his fists clenched, staring after the sound, and Hannah noticed that he was shaking.

Inspector Okoye and Constable Nair arrived within twenty minutes, and the workshop filled with the white flash of cameras and the murmur of professional voices. On the splintered door frame, caught on a protruding nail, Nair discovered a single tiny fibre of dark green cloth, which she lifted with tweezers into a bag. It was a very small thing, but it was the first real thing that the thief had left behind.

Hannah drew a breath and admitted that the black notebook was safe, and that she had been hiding it in a teapot in the dresser at home. She ran back to Marsh Street, fetched it, and handed it to the inspector, who turned the pages slowly and nodded. It was clear that Okoye was not delighted by the delay, but equally clear that she was relieved the notebook had survived.

Okoye asked who had known about the cabinet, and Hannah counted them on her fingers, herself, Owen, the inspector and the constable, and nobody else in the world. Then she understood, with a cold drop of the stomach, that it was not necessary to be told about the cabinet when one has been warned to look. Her visit to Pryce's shop, and her questions, had set him searching for Isla's secrets before she could use them.

Hannah blamed herself bitterly, saying that she had gone blundering into Pryce's shop and woken exactly the danger that Isla had tried so hard to avoid. Owen laid a hand on her shoulder, steady for the first time in days, and told her that Isla would have done precisely the same, and would have been very proud of her. It was the kindest thing anyone had said to her all week, and it helped more than he knew.

At first light Larry Voss turned up at the workshop with his raincoat flapping and his pencil already poised, having caught the news from a police radio in his car. Hannah looked at him for a long moment and then, rather than slamming the door, gave him one sentence, that someone had broken in to keep the truth hidden. He wrote it down slowly, and for once he did not look like a man who was enjoying himself.

Before she left, Okoye took Hannah aside and told her plainly that she was now a target, and that she must lock her doors and never walk alone at night. She posted Constable Nair outside the house on Marsh Street, and that evening a small police car stood under the lamp with a pale face glowing behind its windscreen. Hannah looked down at it from the window and found, to her surprise, that she felt safer.

At three in the morning Hannah came downstairs for a glass of water and found Owen sitting alone in the dark kitchen with his hands over his face. He lifted his head and said, in a voice she hardly knew, that he could not carry the secret a moment longer, and that she deserved the truth about the money. She sat down opposite him in the lamplight and, wisely, did not say a single word to interrupt.

Owen explained that when Thomas Reed's old workshop on Anchor Lane had come up for sale in the spring, the owner, a retired solicitor named Leonard Quill, had agreed to let it go to the family for a fair price. Mr Quill was old-fashioned and mistrusted banks and cheques, so Owen had been paying him in cash, a little at a time, for six months. He had told nobody at all, and above everyone else he had been careful not to tell Isla, who noticed everything.

Owen went upstairs, rummaged in the back of a wardrobe and came down with a small green receipt book, which he laid on the table like a confession. Every payment was entered in it in a spidery hand, with the date, the sum and the signature of Leonard Quill, and the total came very close to the price of the workshop. It was the plainest proof that a man could offer, and she had suspected him.

Hannah put her hands over his and told him that she was deeply, painfully sorry for having doubted him, even for a moment, and that she should have trusted him on the very first day. Owen shook his head with a tired, crooked smile and said that anyone would have doubted a man who behaved as strangely as he had. They sat in the quiet kitchen for a while, and the clocks ticked around them like a kindly audience.

Owen said that he had hidden the plan partly because it was meant to be a surprise for Isla's birthday, which fell in two weeks, and partly out of plain stubbornness. When the police and the newspapers had begun to ask about the money, he added, he had been so ashamed and so frightened that he could not bring himself to explain a surprise to strangers. It had seemed such a private thing, and he had been so unused to putting his feelings into words for strangers.

The next morning Okoye drove out to the cottage of Leonard Quill, an elderly man with a white moustache and a very orderly mind, and went through the receipts with him line by line. Every payment in Owen's green book was confirmed by Mr Quill's own ledger, and he said that he had found Owen to be a most honourable young man. The inspector thanked him, closed the ledger and felt a certain weight lift from her case.

Okoye came to Marsh Street that afternoon and told Owen, in her measured and official voice, that he was no longer the main concern of her investigation. She did not apologise, because she was too careful to, but she shook his hand and added that she would be grateful if he stayed in Saltmere for the time being. Owen thanked her with the grave politeness of a man who has been relieved of a great weight.

Mr Dunn telephoned again that evening, sounding faintly sheepish, and said that the firm would be delighted to have Owen back at his desk whenever he wished, now that the police had made their position plain. Owen thanked him warmly and said, in a quiet but unmistakable voice, that he would not return to work until his wife was found. He put the receiver down gently, as though the telephone itself might break if he were less careful.

Owen drew from his pocket a heavy brass key, bright with handling, and held it up to the window so that Hannah could see it. It opened the door of Thomas Reed's old workshop, he told her, and he had planned to press it into Isla's hand on the night of the Lantern Festival, under the paper lights. He turned it over slowly, and for a moment his face was so naked and so sad that Hannah looked away.

Hannah promised him fiercely that they would find Isla, and that he would give her the key under the lanterns just as he had planned. Owen looked out toward the grey line of the sea and answered, very quietly, that they would find her if she wished to be found. Hannah had no answer to that, though she was beginning to believe that her sister wished to be found by exactly one person in the world.

Okoye called at the house with news that she shared reluctantly, and warned them first that she was telling them as friends and not as an officer. Pryce rented a barn on the outskirts of Thornby, she said, a lonely building at the end of a farm track, but she had no reason that a magistrate would accept for searching it. A suspicion, she reminded them gently but firmly, is never quite the same thing as a warrant, and the law does not bend for good intentions.

Hannah and Owen decided between them that no law prevented two people from taking a drive in the countryside, and that a public lane was a public lane. They set out in Owen's old car, which rattled and wheezed, and parked beside a field gate half a mile from the farm. From there they walked the rest, keeping close to the hedge and speaking in whispers, though there was nobody within a mile.

At the end of the track, standing alone among the rough fields, was a tall grey barn with a roof of sagging tiles. Its windows had been boarded over from the inside, and from the great double doors hung a heavy padlock so new that it still shone in the weak sunlight. Everything else about the place was old and neglected, which made the lock all the more telling.

Hannah found a crack between two of the weathered boards, put her eye to it and waited for her sight to adjust to the dimness within. Slowly she made out a heap of grey blankets, and beneath it the dull gleam of enormous iron wheels with teeth as long as a man's thumb, the unmistakable works of a great turret clock. She stepped back from the wall, white-faced and shaking, and whispered to Owen that the stolen church clock was really here, only a few feet away from them.

An engine suddenly sounded on the lane, growing louder, and Hannah and Owen threw themselves down behind the nearest hedge among the nettles and the wet leaves. A moment later the green van with its pale stripe came bumping up the track and drew to a halt before the barn, scattering a flock of startled sparrows. Neither of them dared to breathe or to move a finger while the engine ticked and cooled and the driver's door swung open above them.

Rufus Dray climbed down from the cab, rattled the padlock to make sure it was secure and spoke into a mobile telephone in a flat, unhurried voice. Hannah, flat on her stomach in the nettles, heard him say that the buyer was due to collect on Monday, and that Mr Pryce wanted the plate found before then, whatever it took. Then he got back into the van and drove away, and the lane was quiet.

Back in Saltmere, Okoye listened to the whole story with her arms folded and an expression that moved from alarm to professional interest. At the end she shook her head and said that a glimpse through a crack in a barn and half a sentence overheard in a hedge were still not enough for a warrant, however true they might be. She would put the matter before a magistrate nonetheless, and she would do it that same afternoon.

Okoye also warned them, with a seriousness that made the corridor seem colder, that Pryce wanted the missing plate quite as badly as they did. If Isla was alive and in hiding, she said, and had the plate, then the man would search for her with every resource he possessed, and he was certainly not short of friends. It was a prospect that neither Hannah nor Owen had allowed themselves to consider.

That night Hannah could not stop thinking about what Okoye had said, and she stood at the window of the spare room watching the wind move the shadows of the lanterns that still hung on a few of the houses. If Pryce found her sister first, whatever the plan had been, nothing at all would be left of it. She would have to solve the puzzle of the stopped clock before he did, and she would have to do it quickly, before the buyer's Monday came.

At last, scanning the black notebook yet again with the lamp pulled close, Hannah turned to the very last page, where she had never thought to look closely. In the bottom corner, drawn in pencil so faintly that it might have been a shadow, were a pair of clock hands standing at twenty to ten, and beneath them, in Isla's unmistakable writing, the words Tick and Hide. It was the clearest message she could have hoped for, and the time was still a riddle.

At dawn, unable to lie still any longer, Hannah walked down to the harbour and stood on the sea wall at the exact place where the red scarf had been found. The tide was out and the mud shone silver, and she asked herself, for the hundredth time, why Isla would have chosen to leave something here, and not in the workshop or at the station. The question buzzed in her mind like a trapped bee, and it felt as though the answer lay very close at hand, almost within reach of her fingers.

Just below the wall, beside the stone steps, a small blue ferry called the Kittiwake lay moored with her ropes creaking gently in the swell. Hannah had known the boat since she was a child, and had taken her out to Gull Island on school trips, but this morning she saw her with new eyes. The scarf had been left a few paces from the place where passengers boarded.

A notice chalked on the weathered board beside the steps announced that in festival week an extra late boat would run to Gull Island for the lantern viewing. The last boat of the evening, it said, would leave the steps at twenty to ten, and the sentence ended with a flourish of chalk. Hannah read the line twice, then a third time, and the world seemed to tilt gently beneath her feet.

In an instant the whole riddle came clear, and she saw that the stopped clock was not a clue about the time of anything but a timetable, a boat that left the harbour steps at twenty to ten. The place it named was Gull Island, exactly as in the old game of Tick and Hide. She laughed aloud on the empty sea wall, a laugh with tears in it, and the startled gulls rose in a screaming cloud from the posts of the quay.

Hannah ran the whole way back to Marsh Street, burst into the hall and stood panting before the row of hooks beside the door. The single empty hook that she had noticed on the first morning, and had so carelessly forgotten, was the place where Isla's grey raincoat with the deep hood always hung, and the raincoat was nowhere in the house. Her sister had put it on that Friday evening and had walked down to the ferry in it, as plain as day.

Hannah told Owen everything in a rush, the clock, the timetable, the empty hook, and as she spoke the colour drained from his face and then came flooding back. He said that Isla's old teacher, Miss Agnes Penhale, lived in a cottage beside the lighthouse on Gull Island, and that Isla had always spoken of her as the one person who had never once doubted her. It was exactly the sort of place where a frightened woman, who needed somewhere to be safe and unfound, might choose to go.

They hurried down to the ferry shed, where old Sam Tully sat on an upturned crate in the doorway with a coil of frayed rope across his knees, working a splice with his thick brown fingers. He looked up at them from under his woollen cap with eyes as pale as sea glass. He listened without interrupting while Hannah asked about the last boat to the island on the night that Isla had gone missing.

Tully scratched his chin and said that he did remember a woman on that last boat, wrapped in a grey hooded raincoat. She paid her fare in cash and sat alone at the stern with a heavy bag on her knees. He could not describe her face, for the hood had been pulled low, but as she stepped onto the island jetty she had told him that she would not be needing the morning boat back.

Tully added, with a certain grievance, that not one policeman had thought to ask him about Friday's boat, and he had supposed that they were only interested in the people who lived on land. He had assumed that the woman was some visitor who had decided to stay on the island, and in all the fuss about the town and the scarf he had quite forgotten about her. Hannah thanked him warmly for remembering, and the old man, who was not used to being thanked, looked rather pleased and a little embarrassed.

As they turned away from the shed, Hannah caught sight of a pale face at the window of Finch's Cafe across the quay, half hidden by a hanging plant. It was Mabel Cray, in her grey cardigan, and she was staring straight at them with an expression that Hannah could not read, and that she would later wish she had understood. In a moment the face withdrew from the glass, and the plant swung gently on its chain as though nobody had ever been there.

Owen telephoned Inspector Okoye at once, but she was at the magistrates' court, and her message service answered with a cool recorded voice. He left a clear message, saying that they had reason to believe Isla was on Gull Island, that he and Hannah were crossing on the next boat and that she should follow when she could. He put the phone away in his pocket with a hand that trembled a little, and they walked together down to the harbour steps.

Hannah packed her bag in two minutes, with the red scarf folded on top, the little brass key in an inside pocket and the black notebook wrapped in a clean cloth beneath them. Owen filled a flask with strong sweet tea, put sandwiches in a paper bag and took the one useful thing he could think of, a torch. They did not talk, because each of them was afraid of hoping too much.

The Kittiwake slipped away from the harbour steps with only half a dozen passengers aboard, two walkers with rucksacks, a woman carrying a basket of groceries and a man with a fishing rod. The sky pressed low and grey over the water, and a fine rain began to blow in from the west. Sam Tully stood at the wheel, steady as a rock, and nodded once to Hannah as though he had been expecting her.

Hannah stood at the rail with the spray in her face and thought of her sister as a girl of eleven, with her hair in plaits, leaning out over this very water and shrieking with delight at the gulls. The low shape of Gull Island slowly grew out of the haze ahead, dark with heather, with the white shaft of the lighthouse standing on its far end. It seemed impossible to Hannah that the laughing child and the vanished woman could be one and the same person.

Owen was quiet and pale, gripping the ferry rail so hard that his knuckles stood out. He confessed to Hannah in a low voice that he was afraid, because Isla had left without a word to him, and perhaps there was a reason for that which he did not yet want to hear. Hannah linked her arm through his and said firmly that nobody lays a trail of clues for someone she does not want to see.

The Kittiwake bumped against the old stone jetty of Gull Island, and Sam Tully threw a rope to a rusty iron ring with a practised flick of the wrist. Hannah and Owen stepped ashore into a cold wind that smelled of seaweed and peat, and the screaming of gulls overhead was so loud that they had to shout. The ferryman told them he would wait at the jetty until the afternoon boat.

A narrow path led up from the jetty through a wide moor of heather and bracken, edged by low stone walls that were furred with lichen. Sheep lifted their black faces to stare at the newcomers with the calm contempt of animals who have the island to themselves, and the wind pressed steadily against Hannah's coat as she climbed. She walked a little faster with every step, and Owen kept pace beside her.

As they climbed, Hannah remembered the school trips that Miss Agnes Penhale had led across the water every summer, the sandwiches eaten on the cliff and the singing on the ferry home. The lighthouse had ninety-nine steps, which each child had been made to count aloud on the way up, and Isla, she recalled, had been the only one to climb them with her eyes shut. It had seemed a good game to them then, and it seemed a stranger and more serious one now that Hannah was walking up the same hill.

At the crest of the hill the lighthouse rose before them in all its glory, white and tall, with its red band like a ribbon about its waist, and at its foot stood a low stone cottage with whitewashed walls. A thread of grey smoke rose from the chimney and was torn away at once by the wind, and a small neat garden, full of bright autumn flowers, lay in the shelter of the wall. Somebody was certainly at home in the cottage, and Hannah's heart began to knock against her ribs as she drew near.

They came to the front door, which was painted a bright cheerful blue, and in the little stone porch beside it, on an iron peg, hung a grey raincoat with a deep hood. Hannah knew it at once, as she knew her own face, and she put out a hand and touched the damp wool as though it might vanish. Owen made a small sound in his throat, took hold of the porch rail and for some moments was quite unable to speak.

Hannah knocked, and after a moment that felt like an hour the blue door swung open. A tall old woman stood there with her white hair pinned up and her spectacles hanging on a chain, and she looked at the two visitors with an expression of mild, dry satisfaction. She said that she had been wondering for days how long they would take, and that she had expected them a good deal sooner.

Miss Agnes Penhale, who had been a schoolteacher for forty years and had never quite stopped, ushered them into the narrow hall with brisk, commanding gestures. She wore a great woollen shawl, thick boots and an air of total competence, and she told them to wipe their feet and mind the clocks. Hannah saw that the hall was crowded with them, grandfather clocks and wall clocks and carriage clocks, ticking in a gentle chorus.

The parlour was warm and low-beamed, with a driftwood fire burning in the grate and a dozen clocks ticking on every surface, and it smelled of tea and beeswax and wool. Miss Penhale stood by the mantelpiece, folded her hands and said, with the faintest softening of her severe face, that somebody in the house had been counting the days. That somebody, she added, would be most relieved to see them, and had been behaving very badly about the cooking.

A door opened at the far side of the parlour, and in the doorway stood a woman, thinner and paler than Hannah remembered, with her dark hair cropped close to her head and a plain jersey hanging off her shoulders. For a long instant nobody spoke or moved, because the sight was too large to take in. It was Isla, and she was alive, and she was looking at them with brimming eyes.

Owen crossed the room in two strides and took his wife in his arms, and the sound that came out of him was neither a word nor a sob but something between the two. He held her so tightly that the fear of a whole fortnight seemed to run out of both of them into the floor, and he buried his face in her cropped hair. Hannah stood by the fire, laughing and weeping at the same moment, with her hands pressed to her mouth.

At last Isla lifted her head from Owen's shoulder, turned to her sister with a shaky smile and whispered, “You found my clock.” Hannah, whose face was wet through, answered, “You stopped it,” and her voice cracked in the middle of the words. Then the two of them were in each other's arms, rocking a little, exactly as they had done as children after a very long game of hide and seek.

When she could speak again Hannah scolded her sister, as only a sister can, for every sleepless night and every terrible thought of the last fortnight. She said that Isla had frightened them half to death, that a clue was one thing and a disappearance was quite another, and that she should be ashamed. Isla bowed her head and said, in a small voice that was not at all like her, that she was truly and humbly sorry.

Owen said gently that people in Saltmere had whispered about him, that the newspaper had hinted he knew something, and that for days he had been the main suspect in his own wife's disappearance. Isla, who had seen no paper and heard no radio on the island, stared at him in dawning horror, with her hand clapped over her mouth. She whispered that she had never imagined it, and had never meant that, not for a single moment.

Miss Penhale, who had seen a great deal of emotion in her time and distrusted it in large quantities, decided that everyone had had quite enough excitement for the moment. She marched into the kitchen, banged the kettle onto the stove and announced over her shoulder that tea always came before explanations. It was the voice that had steadied generations of frightened schoolchildren, and, to Hannah's surprise, it worked on her too.

They all sat down at the old kitchen table with cups of hot sweet tea, and Owen would not let go of Isla's hand for a single moment, not even to lift his cup. Isla looked round at the three faces that were turned toward her, took a deep breath and said that she would begin at the beginning, which was with Gideon Pryce. The clocks ticked softly in the next room, and everybody leaned forward to listen.

Isla explained that about two months earlier a longcase clock had come into Pryce's workshop for cleaning, and that something about its brass maker's plate had bothered her. The number stamped on it was sharper and brighter than the old metal around it, as though somebody had hammered it in only weeks before. She had set the thing aside in her mind, but it kept nagging, as a loose thread nags a tidy person.

Isla spent her free afternoons for weeks in the town library, working through the old trade directories and makers' catalogues that list the numbers of every clock a firm ever produced. She discovered that the numbers on several of the clocks that Pryce had sold simply did not match the records, because they belonged to other clocks, or to clocks that had never existed. The more she checked, the colder she grew, until the library seemed to be as chilly as the bottom of the sea.

At last Isla understood what was happening in the quiet rooms at the back of the shop. Genuine plates were being removed from stolen clocks, new plates with different numbers were being stamped in their place, and false papers were being written that gave each clock an honest and entirely imaginary history. A collector abroad who paid a fortune for such a clock would never guess that it had been stolen from a church or a country house.

One wet afternoon Pryce sent her to the barn at Thornby to fetch a spare spring, and Rufus unlocked the door and left her alone. Under a heap of blankets in the shadows she found the enormous works of a turret clock, and when she wiped the grime from its plate with her sleeve she read the maker's name and the number from the newspaper. It was the great clock of Saint Brannock's, and the old plate was still screwed to its frame.

With a pocket screwdriver and a pounding heart she removed the little brass plate and slipped it into her bag, knowing that without it the clock could not be proved to be the church's. A few days later, while Pryce was out at his long Wednesday lunch and Mabel was upstairs, she copied the pages of his private account book, line by line, onto sheets that she could carry. She kept all of it carefully in an old biscuit tin, together with the plate, in the bottom of her workshop bag.

On Friday at dusk Pryce discovered that the plate was missing, and he came to Isla's workshop in the green van, leaving Rufus waiting at the wheel. He stood in the lamplight, quite calm, and said in his silkiest voice that a pair of careful hands is as easy to break as an old clock, and that he would be sorry to see it happen. Isla felt the hair rise on the back of her neck, and she kept her hands very still upon the bench in front of her.

Isla, with a coolness that surprised even herself, pretended that she was willing to agree to his terms. She said that she had been foolish, that the plate was safely put away and that he should have it on Monday if he would only be patient, and Pryce thanked her smoothly and left. The moment the van drove off, she knew that a man like that would not wait until Monday for anything, and that she had perhaps only a few hours.

Isla knew that she had to vanish at once, so she stopped the tall clock at twenty to ten and hid the little key where only Hannah would think to look. She left her phone in the kitchen drawer so that it could not be traced, and she dropped the red scarf on the sea wall as a second sign. Then, in her grey raincoat with the hood drawn low, she walked down to the harbour steps and boarded the last boat to Gull Island.

Isla said she had told nobody, because Owen was honest and hopeless at lying, and because she was sure that Pryce was watching the house on Marsh Street. She had written to Hannah weeks before, hoping against hope that her sister would come for the festival, since Hannah was the only person alive who could read a stopped clock. It had been, she admitted, a very large gamble on a small game from their childhood.

Isla opened her old bag, took out a bundle wrapped in a piece of soft flannel and laid it on the table beside the teapot. Inside were the two things that had cost her so much, a small brass maker's plate engraved with the name of a Victorian firm and a number, and a biscuit tin crammed with neatly copied pages from Pryce's account book. Nobody at the table said a word, because everybody understood that this was the proof.

Meanwhile, back in Saltmere, Mabel Cray hurried into Pryce's office, wringing her hands, and told him what she had seen from the cafe window, Hannah and Owen at the ferry shed, talking earnestly to old Sam Tully. Pryce listened to her without a flicker of expression, thanked her gently and turned to look at the grey sea. Then, for the first time that week, a slow smile spread across his handsome face.

Pryce counted a fistful of banknotes into Rufus Dray's broad palm, and the pair drove out to the cove at Thornby, where a fisherman asked no questions about the price. They hired a small battered fishing boat called the Gannet, cast off, and set out across the grey water toward Gull Island with the engine thudding. Pryce sat in the stern with his collar turned up, looking like a man on his way to a dinner.

On the island Owen begged his wife to come home with them at once, by the afternoon boat if she could. Isla shook her head gently and said that she wanted to place the plate and the papers directly into Inspector Okoye's hands, because without them nobody would ever believe a word she said. Owen could not argue with that, and he squeezed her fingers and agreed to wait.

Miss Penhale took them out into the little garden and pointed up at the lighthouse, which rose white against the grey sky. Its great lamp was never lit nowadays, she said, except on the night of the Lantern Festival, when the whole town gathered on the shore to watch the beam sweep over the water. This year, because the festival had been postponed, the lamp slept, and the coast was dark.

The telephone signal on Gull Island was poor, so Owen climbed to the top of the hill behind the cottage, holding his phone above his head like a torch. At last the line crackled into life and he heard the voice of Inspector Okoye, very calm, telling him that she had received his message and that the police launch would sail by nightfall, if the court allowed. She asked him to keep everybody together at the cottage, and above all to keep the plate safe.

In the afternoon the two sisters walked out to the cliff edge and sat side by side on the short grass, with the wind pulling at their hair and the sea heaving gently below. For the first time in a year they spoke of the quarrel, quietly and without once raising their voices, each of them taking the blame that belonged to her. It was a strange and windy place to make peace after so long, and it felt to both of them exactly right.

Isla confessed that she had taken the job with Pryce for plain, practical reasons, because their father had left debts and she had wanted to save the workshop, though it had sold anyway. Then the work had turned sour as she learned what her employer was really doing. Hannah took her sister's hand and said that she was sorry for her harsh words that Christmas, which had been cruel, and wrong, and unforgivable.

As the light began to fade, Owen took charge of the stove and made a large and cheerful supper of potatoes, eggs and the last of Miss Penhale's bacon. The kitchen was warm with the smell of frying, and for the first time in two weeks the four of them laughed together at something small. Then Isla froze, her fork halfway to her mouth, because somewhere out over the water they could hear an engine.

Miss Penhale rose and went to the window with the stiff dignity of a general, and looked down toward the island's little jetty, where the last of the daylight lay along the water. A small fishing boat had tied up there, and two men stood on its deck, one of them very big and the other slight, with silver hair that gleamed in the dusk. She turned back to the kitchen and said, in a perfectly even voice, that they were about to have visitors.

Not long afterward there came a knock at the blue front door, firm, polite and perfectly measured, and nobody in the kitchen moved. Isla was the first to rise, pale but steady, and she walked into the hall and opened the door herself. On the step, in a neat dark coat with the dusk behind him, Gideon Pryce smiled and said, “Good evening, Isla.”

Pryce stood in the doorway with a charming smile, hat in hand, while the big shape of Rufus Dray waited behind him in the shadows of the garden. He said, in his most reasonable voice, that he had come a very long way, and that he would be very grateful if Isla would return the small brass plate that she had borrowed. He did not mention the threats he had made, because he did not need to.

Isla, to the astonishment of everyone present, stayed remarkably calm and perfectly polite throughout. She set the flannel bundle and the biscuit tin on the sideboard, well within his sight, and invited Pryce to take the armchair by the fire, saying that he could have the plate in a minute. First, she said, she would very much like to hear how a man of his talent had managed it all, since she had always admired the craftsmanship.

While Pryce was settling himself in the armchair, Hannah slipped into the kitchen and whispered her idea into Miss Penhale's ear, hardly daring to breathe. The old woman's eyes lit up like a girl's, and she nodded once and pointed to a big iron key that hung on a hook beside the back door. It was the key to the lighthouse, and Hannah understood exactly what she was being told.

Isla asked one clever question after another about movements, escapements and the ageing of brass, and Pryce, who adored the sound of his own expertise, began to talk. He boasted that the church clock was the finest piece he had ever handled, that no collector in Europe could tell his work from the original, and that he had never been caught. Owen and Miss Penhale, sitting quietly in the corners of the room, heard every single word that he said, and they remembered it.

Hannah lifted the heavy iron key from its hook, eased the latch of the back door with the gentleness of a burglar and slid out into the cold dusk. Behind her she could hear Isla's voice, steady and curious, and Pryce's pleased and self-satisfied replies, and neither voice faltered. Rufus, she knew, was stationed at the front gate, so she went round the other way, keeping low against the garden wall.

Hannah ran across the moor toward the lighthouse, which stood tall and ghostly pale against the darkening sky. The wind snatched at her coat, the wet heather tore at her ankles, and twice she stumbled and fell, scrambling up again with bleeding palms. She did not let herself think of what would happen if the key did not turn, or if the lamp was broken.

The great key turned in the old lock with a groan, and Hannah stepped into the cold dark tower and began to climb the spiral staircase in the blackness, one hand on the wall. She counted each step aloud under her breath, exactly as she had done as a child on the school trips, and by sixty her lungs were burning and her legs shook. At ninety-nine she stumbled out, dizzy and gasping, into the round glass room at the very top of the tower.

In the glass lantern room the great lamp stood dark and silent, surrounded by its enormous prisms like a sleeping creature wrapped in ice. Beside the iron stair rail, just as Miss Penhale had once shown a class of wide-eyed ten-year-olds, there was a heavy switch protected by a small pane of glass. Hannah broke the pane with her elbow, and the glass tinkled onto the floor.

Hannah seized the heavy switch with both hands and threw it down with all her weight. For an instant nothing happened, and then somewhere deep in the machinery a great hum began to rise, and the lamp came alive in a blaze of white that dazzled her. A beam as thick as a house swung out across the black sea, sweeping the dark waves and the far line of the mainland shore.

On the mainland Inspector Okoye, who had been standing on the harbour quay with a flask of coffee waiting for the court's papers, saw the great white beam swing across the water, and she went very still. Every child in Saltmere knew that the lighthouse lamp burned only on the night of the Lantern Festival, and the festival had been postponed. She dropped the flask, ran for the telephone and ordered the police launch to be ready at once.

In the cottage a bar of white light slid across the parlour window, passed over the ceiling and fell across Pryce's face. He stopped speaking in the middle of a word, and the colour drained slowly out of his cheeks as he understood exactly what it meant. Somebody had lit the lamp, the whole coast could see it, and the one person who would know what it signified was the police.

Pryce leapt from the armchair with a snarl that wiped away all his charm, snatched the biscuit tin and the flannel bundle from the sideboard and ran for the door. In the garden he shouted for Rufus, and the two men pounded down the path toward the jetty with the beam wheeling over their heads. It was the first time that anyone had seen him run, and it was not a dignified sight.

Owen shot out of the door after them, shouting at the top of his voice, while Isla ran behind him calling for him to be careful. Miss Penhale, with remarkable speed for a woman of her years, reached the garden gate before Rufus did and swung it shut in front of him with the remark that nobody was to run through her roses. The big man had to climb over the wall, and that cost him precious seconds.

At the top of the tower Hannah heard shouts coming faintly from far below, and she left the lamp blazing and flung herself down the winding stairs, counting the steps in reverse. Twice she missed her footing in the dark and caught herself on the wall, and her heart hammered against her ribs, but she did not slow down. By the time she burst out of the door at the bottom she was gasping for breath.

Owen proved to be a great deal faster than anyone had expected, an accountant on the run, and he reached the jetty before the others and planted himself in the middle of the narrow stone causeway. He stood with his arms spread wide, a quiet man in a tidy coat, blocking the only way to the Gannet that rocked on the swell below. Behind him, high above the island, the great beam of the lighthouse went on sweeping steadily round across the dark water.

Pryce came panting up the jetty, with his silver hair in disorder and the tin clutched to his chest, and ordered Owen to step aside at once. Owen, who had spent two weeks of his life being suspected of a crime that he had not committed, answered in a clear and steady voice that he would do nothing of the kind. For the first time in all those long weeks he was not afraid of anything that this man could say or do.

Rufus, who had scrambled over the wall and down the steps to the Gannet, looked up and saw a blue light flashing far out across the dark water, coming fast. He was not a quick-witted man, but he was not a stupid one either, and he saw at once that the game was finished. He sat down heavily on the bench of the little boat, put his large hands on his knees and waited for what would come.

Pryce lunged at Owen and tried to shove him aside, but his elegant leather shoes found no grip on the wet boards of the landing stage, and his feet shot from under him. The biscuit tin flew from his arms in a high arc, and Owen, reacting without a thought, put his foot squarely on it a hand's breadth from the edge. It was, as he often said afterwards with a shy smile, the finest piece of footwork that he had ever performed in his whole life.

The police launch came roaring in out of the dark with its engines throbbing and its blue light spinning, and a searchlight swung across the water and fixed upon the jetty. Everybody on the stone causeway was pinned in its white glare like actors on a stage, Pryce on his hands and knees on the boards, Owen with his foot on the tin and Hannah running up, out of breath. There was nowhere left for any of them to run, and every one of them knew it.

Inspector Okoye stepped ashore from the launch as calmly as if she were stepping off a bus. Looking down at the kneeling man, she said, in a level voice, “Gideon Pryce, I am arresting you on suspicion of handling stolen property and of fraud.” Pryce opened his mouth to protest, but nothing came out, and Owen picked up the tin, wiped the damp from its lid and handed it to the inspector with a grave little bow.

That night, in the lamplit parlour of the cottage, Inspector Okoye sat at the kitchen table and took statements from everyone in turn, writing steadily in her notebook. Isla handed over the copied account book from the biscuit tin, and Okoye read it slowly and carefully, page by page, with a small crease deepening between her brows. Every line seemed to lead to another stolen clock, another false paper and another buyer, and she sat back at last with a long breath.

Okoye looked at Isla over the top of the account book and told her sternly that disappearing without a word had wasted a great deal of police time, and caused a great deal of pain. She would not, however, be charged with anything, the inspector said, because the proof that she had gathered was exactly the proof that the police had failed to find. Then Okoye added, with a visible effort, that Isla had been right and she herself had been slow.

At dawn the police launch carried the whole party back across the grey water to Saltmere, with Pryce and Rufus sitting silent under guard in the stern. On the steps of the little police station a figure was waiting in a grey cardigan, white-faced, shivering and clutching a handbag to her chest. It was Mabel Cray, and she had been standing there, as it later turned out, since four o'clock in the morning.

Mabel confessed everything in a rush, weeping, while Okoye listened without interrupting and Constable Nair wrote down every word. For more than a year she had helped to change the plates and type the false papers, because Mr Pryce had frightened her and paid her well. It was she who had telephoned the newspaper about Owen's cash and told him about the ferryman, and she was sorry, and she would give evidence in court.

With the brass plate in one hand and Mabel's signed confession in the other, Okoye went straight to the magistrate, who this time did not make her wait. She left his chambers with a signed warrant to search the barn at Thornby, and with the first real smile that Hannah had ever seen on her face. A few minutes later three police cars were heading out of town, with Hannah, Owen and Isla following in Owen's rattling car.

The police cut through the shiny new padlock with a pair of bolt cutters and swung the big doors wide, letting a long shaft of morning sunlight fall into the dusty barn. In the middle of the floor, under its heap of grey blankets, stood the great turret clock of Saint Brannock's, its iron wheels and brass bearings gleaming faintly as the covers were drawn back. It had waited there since April, patient and silent and perfectly intact, as though it had known all along that somebody would come.

Behind the great clock the police found a dozen wooden crates, each one packed in straw and each holding a beautiful old clock with a shiny newly stamped plate. In a drawer of Pryce's makeshift desk lay an invoice from a foreign collector for a very large sum, with a collection date written plainly across the top, the coming Monday. Okoye read it twice, and then handed it to Constable Nair to be sealed in a bag.

The Reverend Joan Bright was fetched from the vicarage in a police car, and when she saw the old turret clock waiting under its blankets in the barn, she put both hands to her face and wept. Isla stepped forward, took the small brass plate from its flannel and laid it against the empty place on the iron frame, where it fitted exactly, down to the last screw hole. Nobody in the barn could have been in any doubt that this was the church's clock.

The next edition of the Saltmere Gazette carried a very different front page from the one that had hinted so darkly at the husband. Its headline announced that the husband was cleared and the missing wife was safe, and beneath it was a photograph of Isla and Owen standing in front of Miss Penhale's blue door. In one corner Larry Voss had written a short and honest apology to Owen for the things that he had hinted, and it was probably the best piece of writing he had ever done in his whole career.

All that day neighbours knocked at the door on Marsh Street with pies, flowers, casseroles and awkward apologies, and Alma Finch arrived with a lemon cake the size of a cartwheel. Owen forgave everybody with a kind and tired smile, because he was that sort of man, and he said that fear makes people foolish. Hannah forgave them rather more slowly, but she ate the cake, and by the evening she found that she had mostly forgiven them too.

Back on Marsh Street the clocks had run down one by one in the days of her absence, and the house was uncannily silent. Isla went through it with her winding key, bringing each clock back to life in turn, the hall clock, the mantel clock and the cheerful little clock in the bathroom. Last of all she carried the tall clock home from the workshop, set the hands moving and listened with her head on one side to the first tick.

Owen drew the heavy brass key from his pocket and pressed it into Isla's palm, folding her fingers over it with both his hands. He explained, a little breathlessly, that it opened the door of her father's old workshop on Anchor Lane, that the workshop was paid for, and that it was hers. Isla stared at the key and then at her husband, and she did not appear to be able to say a single word.

Together they unlocked the door and walked into the old workshop, where dust hung in the sunlight and the benches stood just as Thomas Reed had left them. Isla ran her hand slowly along the worn wood, and then stopped, because on the inside of the doorframe, carved with a penknife by a small and determined girl, were her own initials, and Hannah's beside them. She laughed and cried at the same time, and so did Hannah, and Owen discovered that he needed to look carefully out of the window.

Hannah, who had been rather quiet over supper, announced that she had applied for a post at the primary school in Saltmere, and that the head teacher had telephoned that very afternoon to invite her for an interview. She said she would like very much to live near her sister, and to see more of her than one Christmas in every two. Isla jumped up from the table, knocked over a glass of lemonade and flung her arms around her.

At sunrise the two sisters sat side by side on the sea wall, with the red scarf folded between them and the tide drawing quietly in below. They spoke of their father, of the long year of silence and of the foolish pride that had kept them apart, and each promised, with a laugh that was also a sob, never again to carry a secret alone. The sun climbed over the harbour, and for the first time in a fortnight the whole world felt gently new.

Volunteers from all over the town, fishermen, schoolteachers, builders and Alma Finch's nephews, carried the great turret clock up the hill to Saint Brannock's on the morning of the festival, wrapped in blankets on a borrowed farm cart. With the vicar watching anxiously and Isla giving orders from the staircase, they lifted it piece by piece through the tower door and up the narrow stair, and bolted it onto the frame. Hannah thought that she had never in her life seen so many people be so gentle and so careful with a single enormous object.

At last the clock was in place, the weights were hung and the great pendulum dangled still in the dusty air of the tower. Isla stood before it for a long moment, laid one hand against the steel and gave it a push so gentle that it seemed hardly to be a push at all. The pendulum swung, and swung back, and the deep slow tick began to roll down the stairs and out into the town like a heartbeat.

On the evening of the postponed festival the whole town gathered by the harbour, and thousands of paper lanterns hung glowing along the quay, on the boats and from every window. Children carried theirs on long sticks, and the lights swayed and bobbed above the crowd like a river of small moons, red and gold and pale green. Even those who never came to the festival came that night, because after such a fortnight the whole town wanted to stand together in the light and feel happy.

Out on Gull Island Miss Agnes Penhale climbed the ninety-nine steps without once stopping for breath, and pulled the great switch in the lantern room as she had done on every festival night for half a century. The lamp woke with a hum, and its white beam went sweeping slowly across the dark water toward the harbour, passing over the lanterns and the upturned faces of the crowd. A great cheer went up from the quay, and it carried across the water like a wave, and the island seemed to answer with a flash.

At ten o'clock exactly the great clock in the tower of Saint Brannock's gathered itself with a whirr and a click, and began to strike, slow and deep and clear, for the first time since April. Its notes rolled out across the harbour and the lanterns and the glittering water, and the crowd fell silent to count them, one, two, three, all the way to ten. Hannah, Isla and Owen stood together in the lamplight, hand in hand, and listened to every stroke of a sound that had been missing from the town for so many months.
